definition: Death of part of the heart muscle because its blood supply is blocked, usually by a clot forming on cholesterol plaque in a heart artery. It is a medical emergency.
Damage to part of the brain when its blood flow is blocked by a clot (ischemic stroke) or a blood vessel bursts (hemorrhagic stroke). Also an emergency — treatment is time-critical.

A long-term condition in which the body does not make enough insulin or does not respond to it properly, so blood sugar stays too high. Over years, high blood sugar damages blood vessels, kidneys, eyes, and nerves.

A state in which the body does not get or cannot use enough energy, protein, or other nutrients, leading to loss of weight, muscle, and strength. In hospital patients it is usually driven by illness and inflammation, not simply by eating too little — and a low albumin level alone does not diagnose it.

Losing body weight without trying. Clinicians grade unintentional weight loss by how much and how fast: about 5% of body weight within six months is mild — and already a warning sign of malnutrition; about 10% within six months is moderate; and over 10% within six months, or 20% or more over a longer period, is severe. The same amount lost slowly grades one step milder. Weight lost on purpose — dieting, or medicines taken for weight — is not graded this way.

A painful form of arthritis caused by uric-acid crystals forming in a joint, most often the big toe. It comes in sudden flares and is treated both by calming the flare and by lowering uric acid over the long term.

Nearest shelves:

The main protein in blood, made by the liver. A low level usually signals inflammation or serious illness rather than poor nutrition, and it is one of the strongest predictors of poor outcomes in hospital patients.

The 'lousy' cholesterol: particles that carry cholesterol into artery walls, where it builds up as plaque. It is the main cholesterol number that treatment aims to lower; the outcome evidence is on the shelves.

A class of cholesterol-lowering medicines that block an enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol, so the liver pulls more LDL out of the blood; a strong statin lowers LDL by about half. Whether that prevents heart attacks and strokes is a trial question — see the shelves.

Blood pressure that stays at or above the level guidelines define as hypertension (130/80 mmHg in the current AHA/ACC guideline). It usually has no symptoms but steadily raises the risk of stroke, heart attack, and kidney damage.

An irregular, often fast heartbeat caused by chaotic electrical signals in the heart's upper chambers. Blood can pool and clot there, which is why AFib raises stroke risk and many patients take a blood thinner.
A life-threatening condition in which the body's response to an infection damages its own organs. It is treated as an emergency with antibiotics, fluids, and support for failing organs.
Kidney damage or reduced kidney function lasting at least three months. Diabetes and high blood pressure are its most common causes, and it raises cardiovascular risk even in its early stages.

A condition in which the heart cannot pump (or fill) well enough to meet the body's needs, causing breathlessness, fatigue, and fluid build-up. It is a long-term condition; how much medicines help is a trial question — see the shelves.
A blood test showing average blood sugar over the previous 2–3 months, reported as a percentage. It is used both to diagnose diabetes (6.5% or higher) and to track control over time.

Blood sugar higher than normal but below the diabetes cut points (A1C 5.7–6.4%). It is a warning zone: the risk of developing diabetes over the following years is substantially higher than at normal levels.

Cholesterol carried by high-density lipoprotein particles, which haul cholesterol from tissues back to the liver. Higher HDL levels tend to travel with lower cardiovascular risk, but HDL itself is not a treatment target.

The main form of fat the body stores and carries in the blood; one of the fats measured on a standard cholesterol panel.

Nearest shelves:

The slow build-up of plaque inside artery walls over years, narrowing the vessels and setting the stage for heart attacks and strokes. Plaque is the deposit itself — cholesterol, fat, calcium, cells, and scar tissue inside the wall; a ruptured plaque can trigger the clot that causes the event.

Weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. Standard bands: underweight below 18.5, normal 18.5–24.9, overweight 25–29.9, obesity 30 and above.

Nearest shelves:
The common joint disease in which cartilage gradually breaks down, causing pain, stiffness, and loss of movement — often called wear-and-tear arthritis.
Inflammation of the appendix, usually set off by a blockage inside it. It causes worsening pain in the lower right abdomen and can lead to rupture if not treated.
A hormone-like vitamin the skin makes from sunlight and that also comes from food. It regulates calcium and bone health, and its blood level is measured as 25-hydroxyvitamin D.

An inactive treatment made to look like the real one — a sugar pill, or even a sham procedure — so a trial can separate a treatment's true effect from the effect of being treated.

Nearest shelves:

A study in which participants are assigned by chance — like a coin flip — to the treatment or to a comparison group. Random assignment is what lets a trial show whether a treatment itself causes the difference in outcomes.

Nearest shelves:

A statistical method that combines the results of several studies asking the same question into one pooled estimate. It is only as trustworthy as the studies it pools.

Nearest shelves:
A waxy, fat-like substance the body needs to build cell walls and to make hormones and vitamin D. It travels in the blood inside lipoprotein particles — mainly LDL and HDL.

Fat building up inside the liver in people who drink little or no alcohol. It is usually silent, travels with excess weight and diabetes, and in some people progresses to liver inflammation and scarring.

Nearest shelves:
An infection of the lungs in which the tiny air sacs fill with fluid and pus, causing cough, fever, and breathlessness.

A decline in memory and thinking severe enough to interfere with daily life. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause; dementia is not a normal part of aging.

Nearest shelves:
Bones lose density and internal structure until they become fragile and can break from a minor fall. It usually develops silently, with a fracture as the first sign.

Too little hemoglobin — the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells — so the blood delivers less oxygen than the body needs. It causes fatigue, pallor, and breathlessness, and it has many causes, from blood loss to kidney disease.

An underactive thyroid gland making too little thyroid hormone, slowing the body's metabolism: fatigue, weight gain, feeling cold, and sluggishness.

Nearest shelves:

An overactive thyroid gland making too much thyroid hormone, speeding the body up: racing heart, weight loss, tremor, and heat intolerance.

Nearest shelves:
Excess body fat, defined by a body mass index of 30 or higher. It is a long-term condition that raises the risk of diabetes, heart disease, fatty liver, and several other illnesses.

Breathing repeatedly stops and starts during sleep, most often because the upper airway closes off (obstructive sleep apnea). It causes loud snoring and unrefreshing sleep, and the severe form strains the heart and blood vessels.

Nearest shelves:

Long-term lung disease — mainly emphysema and chronic bronchitis — in which airflow out of the lungs is permanently narrowed, causing breathlessness and cough. Smoking is the usual cause.

Nearest shelves:

A sudden state of confusion and inattention that fluctuates over hours to days, usually triggered by illness, surgery, or medicines in a vulnerable patient. Unlike dementia it comes on acutely, and it can clear when the trigger is treated.

Nearest shelves:
A blood clot forming in a deep vein, usually in the leg, causing pain and swelling. It is dangerous because part of the clot can break off and travel to the lungs.
A blood clot, usually from a leg vein, lodges in the arteries of the lungs and blocks blood flow. It causes sudden breathlessness and chest pain and is a medical emergency.
Atherosclerosis narrowing the arteries of the legs, causing aching pain when walking (claudication) that eases with rest. It is a sign of artery disease throughout the body.
Chest pain or pressure felt when the heart muscle temporarily receives too little blood, usually because its arteries are narrowed. It is typically triggered by exertion and eased by rest.

A hormone made by the pancreas that lets the body's cells take up glucose from the blood. It is also used as a medicine when the body makes too little of it or needs more help than its own supply gives.

Nearest shelves:

The percentage of blood in the heart's main pumping chamber that is pushed out with each beat; a normal value is roughly 55–70%. Heart failure is classified by whether the ejection fraction is reduced or preserved.

A treatment that does the kidneys' filtering work — removing waste and excess fluid from the blood — when the kidneys have failed, most often with a machine (hemodialysis).

Nearest shelves:

A spreading bacterial infection of the skin and the tissue just beneath it: an expanding area of redness, warmth, swelling, and pain, often with fever.

Nearest shelves:
The main sugar in the blood and the body's quickest fuel. Its level is kept in range by insulin and other hormones, and it is measured fasting, after meals, or as the A1C average.

Blood sugar that has fallen too low (usually below 70 mg/dL), causing shakiness, sweating, confusion, and — if severe — seizures or unconsciousness. It is most often a side effect of diabetes medicines.

Nearest shelves:

Albumin protein leaking into the urine, measured as the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio; normal is less than 30 mg/g. It used to be called microalbuminuria in its mild range — the modern term is simply albuminuria. It is an early sign of kidney damage and also travels with higher cardiovascular risk.

Creatinine is a waste product made by muscle, so its level is also a marker of muscle mass: less muscle means less creatinine, which can make kidney function look better than it is. The kidneys filter it out of the blood, so the blood level is the standard check on kidney function — and it can also be measured in the urine. The eGFR turns the blood level into an estimated filtering rate, scaled to body size.
A waste product made when the body breaks down purines from food and its own cells. When its level stays high it can crystallize in joints (gout) or form kidney stones.
Calcium deposits in the walls of the heart's arteries, measured with a CT scan and reported as a score. It is direct evidence of atherosclerosis in those arteries.
Tissue receiving too little blood flow to meet its needs, so it is starved of oxygen. Ischemia of the heart muscle causes angina and, if prolonged, a heart attack.
Any abnormal heart rhythm — too fast, too slow, or irregular. Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained example.
Inflammation of the pericardium, the thin sac around the heart. It causes sharp chest pain that is often worse lying flat and better sitting forward, and it can come back after the first episode.

Narrowing of the aortic valve, the gate between the heart and the aorta, usually from years of calcium build-up. The heart must push harder to get blood through it. A lifetime of exposure to LDL cholesterol — the total area under the curve over decades — may be related to its development.

Nearest shelves:

A leaking mitral valve: with each beat, some blood flows backward into the heart's upper chamber instead of forward into the body. It can be caused by the valve itself or by a weakened, stretched heart muscle.

Nearest shelves:
A small mesh tube placed inside a narrowed artery and expanded to hold it open, most often in heart arteries during a catheter procedure.
A medicine that slows the blood's clotting system, making clots less likely to form or grow. Warfarin and the direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are the common examples.
A class of medicines that block adrenaline's effects on the heart and blood vessels, slowing the heart rate and lowering blood pressure. Metoprolol and atenolol are examples.

A class of medicines that block the production of angiotensin II, a hormone that tightens blood vessels; vessels relax and blood pressure falls. Lisinopril and enalapril are examples, and a dry cough is a common side effect.
Lab-made versions of cortisol, the body's own stress hormone, used as medicines to reduce inflammation and calm immune activity. Prednisone, dexamethasone, and hydrocortisone are examples.
A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them growing. Antibiotics work only against bacterial infections, not viruses.

The loss of muscle mass and strength that comes with aging and illness. It is measured by grip strength, walking speed, or muscle area on a scan, and it travels with frailty and poor recovery from illness.

Wasting of muscle and body weight, with loss of strength and function, driven by an underlying chronic illness rather than by simply eating too little — feeding alone does not reverse it. A body mass index under 18.5 is one marker of how underweight the person has become. The widely used formal criteria (Fearon, 2011) were developed in cancer patients: weight loss over 5%, or over 2% together with a BMI under 20 or with sarcopenia (low muscle mass).
Live microorganisms, usually bacteria, taken as a supplement or in fermented foods and marketed for gut health. Whether they help any given condition is a trial question — see the shelf.

A state of reduced strength and reserve, usually with aging, in which a minor illness or stress can cause a disproportionate decline. Weakness, slowness, exhaustion, low activity, and weight loss are common features; frailty is not simply old age or disability.

The immune system's response to infection, injury, or irritation. Blood flow and immune cells move into the affected tissue, causing some combination of redness, heat, swelling, and pain; inflammation can be brief and protective or persistent and damaging.

A life-threatening state in which the organs do not receive enough oxygen-rich blood to work properly. It can result from severe infection, blood loss, heart failure, severe allergy, or other causes, and it is different from the everyday use of "shock" to mean emotional distress.
The heart suddenly stops pumping effectively, causing collapse and loss of normal breathing and pulse. It is not the same as a heart attack, although a heart attack can trigger one.

A sudden decline in kidney function over hours to days. By the standard (KDIGO) definition it is present when the blood creatinine rises by at least 0.3 mg/dL (26.5 µmol/L) within 48 hours, or reaches at least 1.5 times its baseline within 7 days, or urine output falls below 0.5 mL/kg per hour for 6 hours. Severe illness, low blood pressure, dehydration, and some medicines are common contributors. Kidney function sometimes recovers and sometimes progresses to longer-term kidney disease.

A blood sodium concentration below the normal range, usually below 135 mmol/L. It most often reflects too much water in the body relative to sodium rather than simply eating too little salt; severe hyponatremia can cause confusion, seizures, and brain swelling.

A blood potassium concentration above the normal range — commonly above 5.0 mmol/L, although the exact upper limit varies by laboratory. Kidney disease and some medicines are common causes; it may cause no symptoms, but it can disturb the heart's rhythm — the classic early sign on an electrocardiogram (ECG) is tall, peaked T waves.

Use of a machine to support or take over breathing, either through a tight-fitting mask or through a tube placed into the windpipe. It is used when illness or injury prevents the lungs or breathing muscles from doing enough of the work alone.

Advanced scarring of the liver that replaces healthy tissue and interferes with the liver's work and blood flow. Causes include viral hepatitis, alcohol, and fatty liver disease; advanced cirrhosis can lead to fluid build-up, bleeding, confusion, and liver failure. Its severity is commonly graded with the MELD (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease) score or the Child-Pugh classification, which groups patients into class A, B, or C.

An infection in the urinary tract, most often in the bladder and less often in a kidney. Bladder infection commonly causes burning with urination, frequency, and urgency; kidney infection more often causes fever and back or flank pain. The classic laboratory criterion is a urine culture growing at least 100,000 bacteria (colony-forming units) per milliliter — the Kass threshold — though in a person with urinary symptoms a true infection can be present at much lower counts, and bacteria in the urine without symptoms (asymptomatic bacteriuria) is not by itself an infection.

A blood potassium concentration below the normal range, usually below 3.5 mmol/L. Water pills (diuretics), vomiting, diarrhea, and poor intake are common causes. It often causes no symptoms, but it can cause muscle weakness and cramps and disturb the heart's rhythm.

A blood glucose level above the normal range. When it persists it is the defining feature of diabetes — a fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or higher on repeat testing is one standard diagnostic threshold. Very high levels can cause dehydration, frequent urination, and, in emergencies, coma.

A state in which the blood is more acidic than normal (arterial pH below 7.35), either because acid builds up or because bicarbonate — the blood's main buffer — is lost or not remade. The lungs and kidneys normally correct it; kidney failure, shock, and diabetic ketoacidosis are common causes.

Abnormally low blood pressure. There is no single defining number for everyone, but in acute care a mean arterial pressure below about 65 mmHg is commonly treated as too low to perfuse the organs. Causes include bleeding, severe infection, dehydration, heart failure, and medicines.

A brief loss of consciousness — fainting — caused by a temporary drop in blood flow to the brain, with recovery on its own within seconds to about a minute. It has many causes, from standing too long to heart-rhythm problems, and it is a common cause of falls in older adults.

A build-up of fluid in the abdomen. The most common cause is cirrhosis, in which scarring raises pressure in the veins feeding the liver and the kidneys retain salt and water. Large amounts cause swelling, discomfort, and breathlessness, and the fluid can become infected. Fun fact (from the developer's own published case report, n of 1, measured serially): abdominal circumference tracks the fluid almost exactly — about 1 cm of girth for every pound gained or lost, or roughly 1 inch per kilogram — so a tape measure can stand in for the scale.

Confusion and other brain dysfunction caused by liver failure: a failing liver does not clear substances — ammonia is the best known — that then affect the brain. It ranges from subtle inattention to drowsiness and coma, and it can come and go.

Difficulty swallowing, of food, liquid, saliva, or pills. Causes include stroke, nerve and muscle diseases, and narrowing or spasm of the esophagus. It raises the risk of food or liquid entering the airway (aspiration) and of not getting enough nutrition.

Nearest shelves:

Too little iron in the body to meet its needs. Iron is essential for making hemoglobin, so deficiency is the most common cause of anemia worldwide; it can also cause fatigue before anemia appears. Blood loss — from the gut or menstruation — poor intake, and poor absorption are the usual causes.

A dangerous complication of diabetes in which a severe lack of insulin makes the body burn fat for fuel, producing acids called ketones that make the blood acidic. About two-thirds of cases occur in type 1 diabetes and about one-third in type 2 — where it is usually set off by infection, another severe illness, or missed insulin. It causes nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, and dehydration, and it is a medical emergency.

Nearest shelves:

The state in which muscle, liver, and fat tissue respond weakly to insulin, so the pancreas has to make more of it to keep blood sugar normal. It is the engine of type 2 diabetes and usually travels with extra weight carried around the waist. Fun fact: blood sugar can stay perfectly normal for years while insulin quietly runs high — the sugar is the last number to move.

A dangerous shift of salts — above all phosphate — into the cells when a starved or severely malnourished person is fed again too quickly. The fall comes fast: phosphate typically bottoms out around the second or third day of feeding, and when it drops below 1 mg/dL (0.32 mmol/L) the heart's rhythm and squeeze are at risk — arrhythmias are the classic fatal event. Lesser falls still weaken muscle, including the breathing muscles, and potassium and magnesium fall alongside. Fun fact: it was first widely described in starved prisoners freed after the Second World War — after starvation, feeding itself has to start slow.

Hard crystals of minerals and salts that form inside the kidney, usually when the urine is concentrated or carries too much calcium, oxalate, or uric acid. A stone that starts moving down the narrow urine tube causes some of the most severe pain in medicine. The usual mix, by main component (Mayo Clinic laboratory, 43,545 first stones): calcium oxalate about 67%, calcium phosphate about 16%, uric acid about 8%, struvite — the infection stone — about 3%, brushite about 1%, and cystine under 1%; the rest are mixed or rarer types. Fun fact: most stones are calcium-based — yet the usual prescription is more water, not less calcium, because calcium in food actually traps oxalate in the gut.

Too little water in the body for it to run well: the blood becomes concentrated, the kidneys strain, and blood pressure can fall. The bedside signs march with the size of the deficit: at roughly 5% of body weight lost, the mucous membranes turn dry — mouth and conjunctiva, with fewer tears; by about 10%, skin pinched into a fold stays up ("tenting") instead of snapping back. In older adults the first signs are often confusion, dizziness, or a fall rather than thirst — and the pinch test itself is unreliable in aged skin, which tents anyway. Fun fact: the thirst alarm weakens with age, so "I'm not thirsty" does not rule it out.

Nearest shelves:

Breathing food, liquid, saliva, or stomach contents into the lungs instead of swallowing them down the food pipe. It can inflame and infect the lung (aspiration pneumonia) and is a particular risk after a stroke or whenever swallowing is weak. Fun fact: many healthy people silently breathe in tiny amounts during sleep — a strong cough and healthy defenses usually clear it without harm.

Nearest shelves:

A body temperature of 100.4 °F (38.0 °C) or higher, produced by the brain's thermostat (the hypothalamus) deliberately raising its set point, usually in response to infection. The messengers are chiefly the cytokines interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor: they switch ON prostaglandin E2 production in the hypothalamus, PGE2 turns the set point up, and the body climbs to the new setting over the next hour or so — shivering and feeling chilled as it goes. (Fever medicines such as aspirin bring the temperature down by blocking that PGE2 step.) Fever is not the same as overheating (hyperthermia), where the set point stays normal and the body simply cannot shed heat. Fun fact: fever is believed to be a beneficial, evolved defense — it has been conserved across vertebrates for hundreds of millions of years, makes life harder for many germs, and speeds the immune response.

Nearest shelves:

The sensation of your own heartbeat racing, pounding, fluttering, or skipping. Most episodes come from extra beats, a brief run of fast rhythm, or simply a normal rhythm noticed in a quiet moment. Fun fact: the "thump" people feel is usually not the extra beat itself — that beat is often too weak to notice — but the stronger beat that follows the pause after it.

A plug of platelets and fibrin — the protein mesh of the blood's repair system — trapping red blood cells inside a vessel. In slow-flowing veins the clots are red-cell rich; in fast-flowing arteries they are platelet rich. Fun fact: a clot is the very same machinery that seals a cut — thrombosis is the repair system firing in the wrong place, inside a vessel that needs to stay open.

Bowel movements that are infrequent, hard, or difficult to pass, often with straining or a sense of incomplete emptying. Fun fact: there is no rule that you must go daily — the normal range runs from three times a day to three times a week, and straining and hardness define constipation better than the calendar does.

Nearest shelves:

The disease of vitamin C deficiency. Without vitamin C the body cannot build collagen properly, so tissues weaken: gums swell and bleed, wounds fail to heal, and joints ache. Fun fact: old, long-healed scars can split open again in scurvy — and James Lind's 1753 shipboard comparison of cures, citrus fruit among them, is often called the first clinical trial.

term: Tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), also known as cachectin
definition:
A cytokine poured out by macrophages when they meet bacterial products such as endotoxin — one of the body's master alarm signals, and a true metabolic switch. It raises the temperature set point (fever), orders the liver to stop making albumin and produce acute-phase proteins instead, and pulls fuel out of muscle and fat to feed the immune response. Switched on for days, this defends against infection; left on for weeks, as in chronic infection or cancer, it produces the wasting called cachexia. Fun fact: the molecule was discovered twice — as "tumor necrosis factor" (named in 1975, for melting tumors in mice) and as "cachectin," the hormone of wasting — until 1985, when the two proved to be one and the same protein. Search the older name, cachectin, to trace the metabolic half of its history.

Nearest shelves:

A long-term lung condition in which the airways are inflamed and overly reactive, narrowing in response to triggers such as allergens, cold air, exercise, or infections. It causes wheezing, cough, chest tightness, and shortness of breath that come and go, and severe attacks can be life-threatening.

Nearest shelves:

A burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain that temporarily disrupts normal function — causing convulsions, staring, confusion, or loss of awareness, depending on the area involved. Most seizures are not the fall-to-the-floor convulsing kind: only about 20–25% (about a quarter) are generalized tonic-clonic ("grand mal") seizures, in which the whole body stiffens and shakes and consciousness is lost. About 60% (three in five) are focal seizures, starting in one part of the brain — twitching, odd sensations, or a trance-like spell with impaired awareness, without convulsions. Absence seizures — brief staring spells, once called "petit mal" — are about 5% (1 in 20), mostly in children. A seizure that continues beyond about five minutes, or repeats without recovery between them, is called status epilepticus and is a medical emergency.

Too little oxygen reaching the body's tissues. It is usually tracked in the blood as oxygen saturation — normally about 95–100% — or as the partial pressure of oxygen (hypoxemia is the blood finding). Lung disease, heart failure, and breathing failure are common causes.

Bleeding anywhere in the digestive tract, from the esophagus to the rectum. Bleeding from the upper tract may cause vomiting of blood or black, tarry stools; bleeding from the lower tract more often causes red blood in the stool. Ulcers, inflammation, abnormal blood vessels, cancers, and blood-thinning or anti-inflammatory medicines are common causes.

Yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes caused by a build-up of bilirubin, the pigment formed when old red blood cells are broken down. It signals that the liver is not processing bilirubin normally, that bile drainage is blocked, or that red blood cells are being destroyed too fast.

The protein inside red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and brings carbon dioxide back. Its blood level is the main measure of anemia — typically about 13.5–17.5 g/dL in men and 12–15.5 g/dL in women, varying by laboratory.

Nearest shelves:

A resting heart rate faster than normal is tachycardia (usually above 100 beats per minute); slower than normal is bradycardia (usually below 60). Either can be a normal response — exercise, fever, sleep, athletic fitness — or a sign of a rhythm problem, especially when it causes dizziness, chest pain, or fainting.

Nearest shelves:

A platelet count below the normal range. Platelets are the blood cells that start clotting; the normal count is roughly 150,000–400,000 per microliter (150–400 × 10⁹/L). Low counts raise the risk of bruising and bleeding; causes include immune destruction, medicines (heparin is a classic), liver disease, and bone-marrow problems.

Nearest shelves:

Swelling caused by excess fluid in the body's tissues, most visibly in the legs and ankles. It has many causes — standing, pregnancy, heart failure, kidney or liver disease, low albumin, and medicines such as some blood-pressure pills — so edema is a sign to explain, not a diagnosis by itself. Fun fact (from the developer's own published case report, n of 1): when the fluid comes off, the tape measure tracks it — about 1 cm off the abdominal circumference for every pound lost, or roughly 1 inch per kilogram — so girth can stand in for the scale.

Nearest shelves:

A vitamin essential for making red blood cells and for healthy nerves, found in meat, dairy, and eggs. Deficiency — from poor absorption (pernicious anemia, stomach surgery, some medicines such as metformin) or a diet without animal products and without supplements — causes anemia and can cause numbness, balance problems, and memory trouble. A very high level is not always reassuring either: besides supplements or injections, a B12 that is still high when rechecked about a month later can be an early marker of cancer or liver disease — in one study, people whose B12 stayed above 1,000 pg/mL developed cancer at about 5.9 times the rate of people with normal levels — while a single high reading that settles, as inflammation can cause, did not carry that risk.

A burning feeling rising from the stomach into the chest, caused by stomach acid washing back into the esophagus (the swallowing tube); when it happens regularly it is called GERD. It is usually worse after meals and on lying down. The trap: heart-attack pain can feel like heartburn, and heartburn medicine should never be used to decide whether chest pain is serious.

Nearest shelves:

Loose or watery stools, usually three or more in a day. Most cases are infections or food-related and settle within a few days; the main danger, especially in children and older adults, is dehydration. Blood in the stool, high fever, or severe pain points to a different problem. One cause worth knowing: antibiotics can let a germ called C. difficile take over the colon and cause severe diarrhea.

Nearest shelves:

Trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early, despite having the chance to sleep. It is different from sleep apnea, where repeated breathing pauses fragment the night. In older adults, sleeping pills are a common quick fix but carry real costs — falls, confusion, and next-day grogginess — so they are a last resort, not a first.

Nearest shelves:

A severe, whole-body allergic reaction that can kill within minutes: the airway swells, breathing tightens, and blood pressure falls. Common triggers are foods such as peanuts and shellfish, insect stings, and medicines. The treatment is an injection of epinephrine (adrenaline), given immediately — antihistamines are too slow and are not a substitute.

Nearest shelves:

Stones that form in the gallbladder, most of them made of cholesterol. Most never cause any symptom at all. When one blocks the gallbladder's outlet it causes attacks of pain in the right upper abdomen, often after fatty meals; a stone that escapes can also block the pancreas duct (see Pancreatitis) or the bile duct (see Jaundice). The lasting fix for troublesome stones is removing the gallbladder.

Nearest shelves:

The feeling of not getting enough air. It is a symptom, not a diagnosis — the main causes are heart failure, lung diseases such as COPD and pneumonia, a blood clot in the lung, anemia, and anxiety. Shortness of breath can also be a sign of angina — the heart not getting enough blood — sometimes the only sign, with no chest pain at all. Breathlessness and low oxygen are different things: a person can feel very breathless with a normal oxygen level, and dangerously low oxygen sometimes causes little breathlessness at all — which is why both the feeling and the measurement matter.

Nearest shelves:

Inflammation of the pancreas, usually causing severe upper-abdominal pain that often bores through to the back, with nausea and vomiting. The two commonest causes are gallstones and alcohol; very high triglycerides are a third. Most attacks settle with fluids and rest, but severe attacks can destroy pancreatic tissue and become life-threatening. Fun fact: The pancreas makes enzymes strong enough to digest food — in severe pancreatitis they switch on inside the gland itself, and it begins, in effect, to digest itself.

Inflammation of a diverticulum — a small pouch in the wall of the colon. It causes pain, usually in the left lower abdomen, often with fever. Most uncomplicated attacks were long treated with antibiotics for every patient; two randomized trials found that selected patients do just as well without them.

The illusion that you or the room is spinning. The commonest cause is BPPV — loose crystals in the inner ear — which triggers brief spins, under a minute, when the head moves in certain ways, and is treated with repositioning maneuvers rather than medicine. Vertigo that is constant, or comes with slurred speech, weakness, or double vision, can be a stroke and is an emergency. People often say "dizzy" for lightheadedness too, which is a different problem — see Syncope.

Nearest shelves:

A cluster of findings that travel together and carry a very high cardiovascular risk, along with a raised risk of type 2 diabetes: a large waist, high triglycerides, low HDL cholesterol, raised blood pressure, and raised blood sugar. The usual rule is any three of the five. It is not a separate disease so much as a warning pattern — the same cluster that insulin resistance produces.

The feeling of being about to vomit. It is a symptom with many causes — stomach and gut infections, motion, migraine, pregnancy, medicines (chemotherapy and opioids are common ones), and problems deeper in, from a blocked bowel to raised pressure inside the skull. Nausea that keeps happening, or comes with vomiting blood, severe pain, or weight loss, needs a diagnosis, not just a pill for the feeling.

Nearest shelves:

A reflex that clears the airways — one of the body's basic defenses, and one of the commonest reasons people see a doctor. Most coughs come from colds and settle in two to three weeks. A cough lasting more than eight weeks in an adult is called chronic and deserves a search: the commonest causes are postnasal drip, asthma, and acid reflux — and in smokers, COPD and lung cancer enter the list. Coughing blood is never normal and is always a reason to be seen promptly.

Nearest shelves:

A musical, whistling sound made by air moving through narrowed airways — and which part of the breath it rides on tells you where the narrowing is. A musical sound on breathing out (a rhonchus) points to the airways in the chest: asthma is the classic cause, and COPD, heart failure (sometimes called cardiac asthma), and an allergic reaction can all do it too. A harsh, raucous sound on breathing in (stridor) points higher — the throat and windpipe — and is more often an emergency. In a small child, a first episode with a chest infection is usually a virus or bronchiolitis. One warning sign matters: in a bad asthma attack, a chest that goes quieter is getting worse, not better — less air is moving.

Nearest shelves:

Involuntary spasms of the diaphragm — the main breathing muscle — each followed by the vocal cords snapping shut, which makes the "hic" sound. Attacks lasting minutes are usually triggered by a full stomach, fizzy drinks, alcohol, or excitement, and stop on their own. Hiccups lasting more than 48 hours, or ones that keep coming back, are a different matter: they can signal irritation of the vagus or phrenic nerves, reflux, or a problem in the brain, and they deserve a workup rather than home remedies.

Nearest shelves:

Hearing a sound — ringing, buzzing, hissing — that is not there. It usually travels with hearing loss, most often from age or noise damage. Tinnitus that pulses in time with the heartbeat is different and can point to a blood-vessel problem, and tinnitus in one ear only should be checked. No pill is proven to cure it; the mainstays are treating any hearing loss, sound therapy, and retraining attention so the sound fades into the background even when it does not disappear.

Nearest shelves:

A pain in the head — one of the commonest symptoms there is. Most headaches are tension-type or migraine and are not dangerous. A short list is different and means get seen now: a sudden "thunderclap" headache that peaks within a minute; the worst headache of your life; headache with fever and a stiff neck; headache after a head injury; a new headache after age 50; or headache with weakness, confusion, or vision change. Headaches that are new, changing, or waking you from sleep also deserve a workup rather than another painkiller.

Nearest shelves:

Tiredness that rest doesn't fix. It is different from sleepiness — the urge to fall asleep — though the two often travel together and are worth telling apart, because they point in different directions. Fatigue is a symptom, not a diagnosis: common causes include anemia, an underactive thyroid, depression, heart failure, and sleep apnea — which causes sleepiness first and fatigue second. Fatigue that persists for weeks, or comes with weight loss, fever, or breathlessness, deserves a search for its cause.

Nearest shelves:

A rough, strained, or weak voice, caused by something affecting the vocal cords in the larynx (voice box). The usual causes are laryngitis from a cold, acid reflux reaching the throat, and voice overuse. Hoarseness lasting more than three weeks needs the cords looked at directly — especially in smokers — because a growth on the cord, including cancer, is on the list and is most curable when caught early.

Nearest shelves:

The urge to scratch. When there is a rash, the cause is usually in the skin itself — eczema, dry skin, allergy, hives, or infection. Itching all over with no rash is a different clue: it can come from the liver (bile backing up), failing kidneys, an over- or underactive thyroid, low iron, or, uncommonly, a lymphoma. Whole-body itching that doesn't settle deserves blood tests, not just a stronger cream.

Nearest shelves:

The noise made when the relaxed tissues of the throat vibrate during sleep. It is very common and often harmless in itself. It becomes a medical matter when it travels with witnessed pauses in breathing, choking or gasping arousals, or daytime sleepiness — the signature of sleep apnea, which is hard on the heart. A bed partner's report of pauses is worth more than the snore's volume: loud is common, pauses are the warning.

Nearest shelves:

An unsteady, lightheaded, or faint feeling — one word patients use for several different sensations, and telling them apart is most of the diagnosis. Spinning, where the room seems to move, is vertigo — an inner-ear problem. Feeling about to faint, especially on standing, points to blood pressure drops, dehydration, blood loss, or a heart rhythm problem. A vague unsteadiness in an older person usually has several small causes at once — medicines, vision, nerves, balance. New dizziness with weakness, slurred speech, or double vision is a stroke until proven otherwise.

Nearest shelves:

Any change in the skin's look or feel — redness, bumps, blisters, scaling. Most rashes are local problems: eczema, allergy, infection, or irritation. A rash turns urgent with blistering or skin pain (the skin itself is failing), with fever plus a rash that does not fade under pressure (possible meningitis or sepsis), or with swelling of the lips and tongue (an allergic reaction turning dangerous). A new rash after a new medicine is a drug reaction until proven otherwise — the medicine list is the first place to look.

Nearest shelves:

Pain in the back, most often the low back — one of the commonest reasons for a doctor visit and for missed work. The great majority is mechanical (muscle, joint, disc) and improves within weeks without any scan; early imaging mostly finds age-normal wear that was not the cause. The red flags that change everything: leg weakness or numbness in the saddle area, loss of bladder or bowel control (a surgical emergency), fever, a history of cancer, major trauma, or pain worst at night and unrelieved by rest.

Nearest shelves:

Pain in one joint or many — and the count matters. One hot, swollen joint is an emergency until proven otherwise: it can be infection, which can destroy the joint in days, gout, or bleeding into the joint. Many painful joints with morning stiffness that comes back the same every day and lasts over an hour — especially in the hands, which patients say feel "like they're in wax" until it loosens — points to inflammation, rheumatoid arthritis and its relatives, where early treatment prevents permanent damage. The commonest cause overall is osteoarthritis, wear-and-tear: brief morning stiffness, aching with use, easing with rest.

Nearest shelves:

Loss of feeling, or the abnormal tingling called pins and needles. Where it sits tells the story: one hand's fingers suggest a pinched nerve at the wrist (carpal tunnel); both feet, symmetrically, suggest a nerve problem from diabetes, alcohol, or low vitamin B12; one patch on a leg follows a single nerve root from the spine. Sudden numbness on one side of the face or body is a stroke until proven otherwise. Numbness that climbs, or comes with weakness, needs same-day care.

Nearest shelves:

A bruise is blood leaked from tiny vessels under unbroken skin, usually after a knock — it changes color as the blood is cleaned up, from red-purple through green-yellow, over about two weeks. Easy bruising has everyday causes: aging skin and the sun damage that thins it, steroids, and blood thinners, aspirin, and some supplements. Bruising earns a workup when it appears without injury, is unusually large or painful, comes in crops, or travels with bleeding gums, nosebleeds, or blood in the urine or stool — that pattern points at the platelets or the clotting system itself.

Nearest shelves:

True weakness means loss of muscle strength — trouble rising from a chair, lifting an arm, keeping a grip — and it is different from fatigue or feeling unwell, a distinction that steers the whole workup. Pattern tells the story: sudden weakness on one side of the body is a stroke until proven otherwise; weakness that climbs from the feet over days (Guillain-Barré) is an emergency; weakness that worsens with use and eases with rest points to the nerve–muscle junction, as in myasthenia. Many medicines can make muscles ache without truly weakening them — aching and weakness are not the same complaint.

Nearest shelves:

An involuntary, rhythmic shaking, most often of the hands. The commonest cause is essential tremor: present with action — holding a cup, writing — often running in families, sometimes quieted by a little alcohol; benign, though it can disable. Parkinson's tremor is the opposite pattern: worst at rest, easing with action, usually starting on one side, with slowness and stiffness for company. A new or changing tremor can also come from an overactive thyroid, caffeine, low blood sugar, or medicines — lithium and some asthma and antidepressant drugs among them.

Nearest shelves:

Losing hair beyond the normal shed of roughly 50–100 hairs a day. Pattern tells the kind: gradual thinning at the temples and crown in men, and over the crown in women, is the hormone-and-heredity kind — by far the commonest. Round, smooth bald patches are alopecia areata, an immune attack on the follicle. A heavy shed two to three months after a fever, serious illness, surgery, or childbirth is telogen effluvium — the follicles were shocked into resting together — and it usually regrows on its own. Hair loss with scaling, pain, or scarring needs a dermatologist, because the scarring kinds destroy follicles permanently.

Nearest shelves:

Too little saliva. The commonest cause by far is medicines — hundreds list it, from antidepressants and blood-pressure drugs to antihistamines and bladder medicines — followed by mouth-breathing, radiation to the head and neck, and Sjögren's, an immune disease that dries the eyes too. It is not a small thing: saliva protects the teeth, so a dry mouth rots teeth fast, and it blunts taste and makes swallowing dry food hard. Treatment aims at the cause, plus saliva substitutes, sugar-free gum, and aggressive dental care.

Nearest shelves:

Sweat is the body's cooling system — glands release water onto the skin, and its evaporation carries heat away. Too much sweat (hyperhidrosis) usually runs in families and sticks to the palms, soles, and armpits. Sweating everywhere, or drenching night sweats that soak the sheets, is a different signal: a fever breaking, menopause, an overactive thyroid — or, on the serious list, tuberculosis and lymphoma. A cold, clammy sweat with chest pressure or breathlessness is a heart-attack warning until proven otherwise.

Nearest shelves:

Vision that loses its sharpness. Gradual blurring in both eyes is usually focus — glasses, cataracts, or, in diabetes, sugar swelling the lens (that kind can swing day to day with the glucose). Sudden blurring is different: in one eye it can be a blocked retinal vessel or a detaching retina (watch for flashes, a shower of floaters, or a curtain over the view); in both eyes, or with weakness or speech trouble, it can be a stroke. Any sudden vision loss is an emergency — retina and brain both worsen by the clock.

Nearest shelves:

Pain or pressure in the chest — the symptom nobody should grade at home. Heart pain (angina) is typically a heavy pressure or squeezing across the center, brought on by effort or emotion, easing with rest, sometimes spreading to the arm, jaw, or back; a heart attack's pain lasts, and often brings sweating, nausea, or breathlessness. But the chest holds more than the heart: reflux burns, chest-wall muscle aches sharply with movement, pleurisy stabs with each breath, and a torn aorta — rare and catastrophic — rips through to the back. Because the worst cause is common and time-critical, new chest pressure means an emergency call, not a wait-and-see.

Nearest shelves:

Trouble remembering — names, dates, where things are. Some is normal aging: slower recall, the word on the tip of the tongue — while judgment and daily function stay intact. Memory loss that erodes daily life — repeating questions, getting lost in known places, bills going unpaid — is not normal aging; the mild stage is called mild cognitive impairment, and the advanced stage is dementia, most often Alzheimer's disease. Sudden confusion over hours to days is a different emergency — delirium, usually from infection, dehydration, or medicines. Reversible causes are always worth hunting: low vitamin B12, thyroid trouble, depression, poor sleep, and the medicine list.

Nearest shelves:

A clouded, muddled mind — trouble thinking clearly, paying attention, or knowing where you are. When it comes on suddenly, over hours or days, and waxes and wanes, it is delirium: the brain's alarm bell, almost always with a physical cause — infection, dehydration, low or high blood sugar, medicines (new ones first), alcohol withdrawal, or a stroke. Delirium is an emergency, especially in older people, in whom it may be the only sign of a serious illness. Confusion that creeps in over months to years is a different road — the dementia workup.

Nearest shelves:

Throwing up — the forceful emptying of the stomach. It partners with nausea but is its own event, driven from a vomiting center in the brain that takes reports from the gut, the inner ear, the blood (toxins, medicines, hormones), and the brain itself. Most episodes are stomach infections or food poisoning and pass in a day or two. The red flags: blood or coffee-ground material; vomiting with a severe headache or stiff neck; signs of dehydration — dry mouth, little urine, dizziness on standing; nothing kept down for more than a day; and, in a young infant, vomiting that shoots out forcefully.

Nearest shelves:

A burning feeling rising behind the breastbone, from stomach acid washing up into the esophagus — which, unlike the stomach, has no armor against acid. Occasional heartburn after a big, late, fatty meal is nearly universal. Heartburn twice a week or more is GERD, and years of it can scar the esophagus narrow or change its lining (Barrett's esophagus), a step toward cancer. Alarm features mean a scope, not another antacid: trouble swallowing, food sticking, weight loss, vomiting, or black stools. And the standing trap: heartburn and heart pain overlap — pressure with exertion, sweating, or breathlessness is the heart until proven otherwise.

Nearest shelves:

A feeling of fullness, tightness, or visible swelling of the belly — usually gas: swallowed air, gas-producing foods, a bowel that moves slowly, or a gut that senses stretch too keenly, as in irritable bowel syndrome. Most bloating is uncomfortable, not dangerous. It earns a workup when it is new and persistent in an older person, or comes with weight loss, vomiting, or blood in the stool — and a belly that keeps steadily growing may be fluid (ascites) or a mass, not gas at all.

Nearest shelves:

Reduced hearing, in one ear or both. It comes in two mechanical kinds: conductive — sound is blocked on its way in, by wax, fluid behind the eardrum, or stiffened middle-ear bones — and sensorineural — the inner ear or its nerve is damaged, by age, noise, or certain medicines. Sudden hearing loss in one ear over hours to days is an emergency: treated with steroids within days, some people recover; waited on, most do not. Gradual loss in both ears is usually aging, and hearing aids help more the earlier they are fitted — untreated loss isolates people and tracks with faster cognitive decline.

Nearest shelves:

Eating less because food has lost its appeal. Doctors call it anorexia — which in this medical sense means loss of appetite, not the eating disorder anorexia nervosa. It rides along with almost any illness: infection, cancer, heart or kidney failure, depression, dental trouble, and many medicines. In an older person, a fading appetite is often the first and only sign that something is wrong. New appetite loss with weight loss over weeks always deserves a search — teeth and swallowing, mood, medicines, and malignancy are all on the list.

Nearest shelves:

The urge to fall asleep during the day, in situations where you should be awake. It is different from fatigue — tiredness that rest doesn't fix — and telling the two apart matters, because they point in different directions. The usual causes are simply too little sleep, sleep apnea (breathing that stops and restarts all night), sedating medicines, an underactive thyroid, and depression. Falling asleep at the wheel, or mid-conversation, is a safety problem to fix, not a character flaw.

Nearest shelves:

Blood in the urine, either visible — pink, red, or cola-colored — or found only on a lab test. Common causes are a urinary infection, kidney stones, an enlarged prostate, and, temporarily, hard exercise. The cause that must never be missed is cancer of the bladder, kidney, or prostate, which is why any episode of visible blood earns a workup even if it happens once and stops — painless visible blood, oddly, is the more worrying kind.

Nearest shelves:

Blood passed with or in the stool. Bright red blood usually comes from low in the bowel — hemorrhoids and small tears are the commonest causes, then diverticulitis, inflammation, and polyps. Black, tarry stool is blood that has been digested on its way down from the stomach or upper bowel, and it is the more urgent sign. In an older person, new blood in the stool should never simply be blamed on hemorrhoids without checking — and blood thinners raise the stakes of any of it.

Nearest shelves:

Pain anywhere in the belly, between the ribs and the pelvis. Where it sits, when it comes, and what it feels like are most of the diagnosis: common causes run from gas and constipation to appendicitis (low right side), gallstones (upper right, after meals), a blocked bowel, and, in women who could be pregnant, a pregnancy growing outside the womb. A rigid, board-like belly, pain with fever or repeated vomiting, vomiting or passing blood, or sudden severe pain unlike anything before it — those are emergencies, not wait-and-see.

Nearest shelves:

Needing to pass urine more often than is usual for you, by day or by night (waking to urinate is called nocturia). The classic cause to check first is high blood sugar — the kidney spills the extra sugar and water follows it. Others: a urinary infection, an enlarged prostate, an overactive bladder, caffeine, and water pills (diuretics) doing their job. New frequency together with unusual thirst and weight loss means check the glucose.

Nearest shelves:

Leaking urine that you cannot control. The main types: stress leakage, when a cough, laugh, or lift squeezes it out; urge leakage, when the need comes so suddenly there is no time; and overflow, when the bladder never quite empties. Causes include a weakened pelvic floor, an enlarged prostate, nerve problems from diabetes or stroke, and some medicines. It is common and usually treatable — it is not an inevitable part of growing older, and it is always worth mentioning out loud.

Nearest shelves:

A muscle — most often the calf — suddenly tightening into a hard, painful knot, classically at night in bed (nocturnal leg cramps). Most in older adults have no single cause found. The suspects worth checking: dehydration, low potassium or magnesium, medicines including water pills, and pregnancy. Statins do not belong on this list: they do not cause cramps — the muscle complaint statins cause is achiness, usually on both sides. The immediate fix is mechanical — stretch the muscle the opposite way (pull the toes up for a calf cramp). A cramp that comes with a swollen, warm leg is a different problem — possible blood clot — and needs same-day care.

Nearest shelves:

Coming to rest on the floor or ground without meaning to. In an older person a fall rarely has one cause: usually several small ones at once — blood-pressure or sedative medicines, blood pressure that drops on standing, weak muscles, poor vision or balance, and hazards at home. A fall is a symptom worth investigating, not just bad luck: the review starts with the medicine list. One fall that breaks a hip can cost a person their independence, which is why the cause hunt matters more than the bruise.

Nearest shelves:

Wanting to drink far more than usual, and still feeling thirsty (the medical word is polydipsia). Its classic partner is frequent urination, and together they are the textbook first sign of diabetes: high blood sugar pulls water out through the kidney, and thirst is the body asking for it back. Other causes: dehydration from any source, high blood calcium, certain medicines that dry the mouth, and, rarely, a hormone problem (diabetes insipidus) where the kidney cannot hold water at all. New thirst with frequent urination and weight loss: check the glucose first.

Nearest shelves:

Pain, scratchiness, or rawness in the throat. Most sore throats are viruses — the common cold above all — and heal on their own in a few days. The bacterial one that matters is strep throat, because treating it prevents rheumatic fever, a heart complication that mainly threatens children. Acid reflux, allergies, and dry air make throats sore without any infection. The red flags: drooling or being unable to swallow, a muffled "hot potato" voice, swelling on one side only, or any trouble breathing — same-day care.

Nearest shelves:

Sweating at night heavy enough to soak your nightclothes or the sheets and wake you — not just feeling warm under the covers. Common causes are menopause (hot flashes happening at night), infections — tuberculosis and HIV are the classic ones — some cancers, lymphoma above all, and fever medicines wearing off. Drenching night sweats that keep happening, especially with weight loss or fever, deserve a search, not just a fan.

Nearest shelves:

A sudden wave of heat spreading over the face, neck, and chest, with flushing and sweating, lasting a minute or a few and then passing. They are the signature symptom of menopause, arriving as estrogen falls, and the same thing happens with hormone-blocking treatments for breast and prostate cancer. Other causes: an overactive thyroid and some medicines. At night, hot flashes are what night sweats are made of, and broken sleep is often the worst of it. Frequent or severe flashes are treatable — and new hot flashes in a man who is not on hormone treatment deserve a look for a cause.

Nearest shelves:

Lymph nodes — the "glands" in the neck, armpits, and groin — are filters packed with immune cells. When one swells, it is usually doing its job, fighting an infection nearby: a sore throat swells the neck nodes. Most shrink back within two to four weeks. Pain is a useful first guide: a tender, painful node is usually infection or inflammation — the node is busy fighting. A painless node that stays swollen is the more worrying kind, because painless enlargement may be cancer — lymphoma, or cancer that has spread. The pattern that always earns a workup: a node that keeps growing, feels hard and stuck in place, sits above the collarbone, or is still swollen after a month — especially with fever, night sweats, or weight loss. That node needs an examination, and sometimes a biopsy.

Nearest shelves:

Pain in or around the ear (doctors call it otalgia). In children it is usually a middle-ear infection behind a cold; in adults the commonest causes are earwax, an outer-ear infection (swimmer's ear), jaw-joint strain, and referred pain — the ear shares its nerves with the teeth, jaw, and throat, so trouble there can report to the ear. Get seen promptly for: swelling or tenderness behind the ear, ear pain with hearing loss or dizziness, bloody discharge, or — in an adult — one-sided ear pain that persists while the ear itself looks normal, because the throat then needs the look.

Nearest shelves:

A nose that drips, blocks, or does both (rhinitis). Usually it is the common cold — viral, a few days, done — or allergies, which add sneezing and itchy, watery eyes and follow the seasons or a dusty room. A sinus infection joins the list when there is face pain or pressure with thick discharge lasting beyond ten days, or symptoms that were improving and then worsen. One-sided blockage or bleeding that persists in an adult is not allergies and needs a look inside. And decongestant sprays used daily for more than a few days can cause the stuffiness themselves — rebound congestion.

Nearest shelves:

Bleeding from the nose (epistaxis), usually from the fragile little vessels at the front of the septum. Dry air, hard nose-blowing, colds, blood thinners, and high blood pressure all make it likelier. First aid that actually works: sit up, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of the nose shut for a full ten to fifteen minutes without peeking. It is an emergency if the bleeding won't stop after twenty to thirty minutes of proper pressure, if blood is running steadily down the throat, or if it follows a head injury — and repeated one-sided nosebleeds in an adult need a look inside the nose.

Nearest shelves:

Blood coughed up from the airways or lungs (hemoptysis) — anything from pink-flecked mucus to frank red blood. It is not the same as vomiting blood, which comes from the stomach and often looks like coffee grounds. The commonest cause is bronchitis, in small amounts; the ones that must be found are pneumonia, tuberculosis, a blood clot to the lung (pulmonary embolism), and lung cancer. Any coughing up of blood deserves prompt evaluation — and more than a few teaspoons of it, or any with breathlessness or chest pain, is an emergency.

Nearest shelves:

Vomiting blood (hematemesis) — bright red, or dark and grainy like coffee grounds, which is blood partly digested by stomach acid. The sources: stomach and duodenal ulcers, a stomach lining inflamed by alcohol or pain relievers (NSAIDs), a small tear from hard retching, and — in liver disease — swollen veins in the gullet (varices) that can bleed massively. Vomiting blood is always an emergency, full stop; faster still if there is dizziness, faintness, or black stools.

Nearest shelves:

Losing sight in one or both eyes, partly or completely, suddenly or over time. The gradual, painless causes are cataracts, macular degeneration, glaucoma, and diabetes damage. Sudden painless loss in one eye is an emergency: a blocked retinal artery is a stroke of the eye, and a shadow or curtain coming down suggests the retina has detached. Sudden vision trouble in an older person with a new headache or jaw pain when chewing points to giant cell arteritis — same-day treatment protects the other eye. And vision change that arrives with weakness or speech trouble is a stroke until proven otherwise.

Nearest shelves:

Smell and taste fading or vanishing together — they travel as a pair because most of what we call flavor is actually smell. The usual causes are a cold, flu, or COVID stunning or blocking the nose, and most people recover in weeks. Also on the list: nasal polyps and sinus disease, a head injury, some medicines — and, years ahead of other signs, loss of smell can be an early symptom of Parkinson's or Alzheimer's disease. Loss that persists after an infection clears, or that comes with one-sided blockage or nosebleeds, needs an ear-nose-throat look. The practical hazard is what you can no longer detect: smoke, gas leaks, and spoiled food — check the detectors.

Nearest shelves:

Burping: air from the stomach let out through the mouth. Nearly all of it is swallowed air — eating fast, talking while eating, fizzy drinks, chewing gum — and a CPAP machine can push air into the stomach overnight the same way. Acid reflux is the other common driver. Belching alone is almost never serious; it earns a workup when it arrives with weight loss, repeated vomiting, trouble swallowing, or black stools.

Nearest shelves:

Gas passed from below (flatulence) is a normal product of a working gut — everyone passes it many times a day. It comes from two sources: swallowed air, and gut bacteria fermenting what you couldn't digest — fiber, beans, milk sugar (lactose), and the sugar alcohols in "sugar-free" sweets. Some medicines add to it; metformin is a well-known one. Gas becomes a symptom worth chasing when it comes with blood in the stool, weight loss, persistent diarrhea, or severe pain — or when a sudden change in it is really a change in the bowel habit.

Nearest shelves:

Damage to skin and the tissue under it, over a bony point — heels, tailbone, hips — caused by lying or sitting in one position too long: the pressure squeezes the blood out, and the tissue starves. They start as redness that doesn't fade when pressed and can deepen, in the worst cases, to muscle and bone, where infection follows. The risk rises with immobility, diabetes, poor circulation, and poor nutrition. Prevention beats every treatment: repositioning on a schedule, cushions that spread the load, and daily skin checks. An open sore in someone who is mostly in bed or a chair needs care early, while it is still shallow.

Nearest shelves:

Feeling cold and shivering — the muscles shaking to manufacture heat — as the brain's thermostat turns the set point up at the start of a fever. A hard rigor, with teeth chattering and the whole body shaking, is the classic herald of bacteria loose in the bloodstream; kidney infections and malaria shake the same way. Shaking chills with a fever mean infection until proven otherwise. And in an older or frail person, chills alone — no measured fever — can be the fever equivalent, and deserve the same respect.

Nearest shelves:

Burning or stinging when you pass urine (dysuria). The commonest cause is a urinary infection, usually with needing to go often and urgently. The rest of the list: sexually transmitted infections (especially in younger people, and often with discharge), bladder or kidney stones, an inflamed prostate, irritation or dryness of the vagina after menopause, and some medicines. Pain with fever and back pain means the infection may have reached the kidney — prompt care. And painful urination that keeps coming back in a man always earns a prostate and bladder workup.

Nearest shelves:

An urge to move the legs that is hard to resist, worse when sitting or lying still, worst in the evening, and relieved — while it lasts — by moving. It wrecks the start of sleep. The first thing to check is iron: low iron stores (a low ferritin) cause it even without anemia. Also on the list: kidney failure, pregnancy, caffeine, and some antidepressants and antihistamines. Treatment starts with the iron and the triggers — not with sedatives.

Nearest shelves:

Putting on weight over time. The speed tells the story: gain over days is almost always water, not fat — a failing heart, kidneys, or liver holding fluid — while gain over months is tissue. The usual drivers of the slow kind are eating more than you burn, too little movement, an underactive thyroid, and a long list of medicines: steroids, insulin, some diabetes and psychiatric drugs. Fast gain with new breathlessness or swelling is a same-week problem, not a diet problem.

Nearest shelves:

Pain in the neck — usually strained muscles and worn joints: sleeping in a bad position, hours at a screen, arthritis of the neck bones. Most neck pain settles in days to a few weeks, and gentle movement helps it more than rest does. The red flags: neck pain after an injury; neck pain with fever and a stiff neck that will not bend (meningitis); and neck pain with weakness or numbness running into the arms, clumsy hands, or unsteady walking — pressure on the spinal cord, which is urgent.

Nearest shelves:

Seeing two of one thing (diplopia). One test sorts it: cover one eye. If the doubling is still there with one eye open, the problem is in that eye itself — lens or cornea. If it vanishes whichever eye you cover, the two eyes are no longer pointing together — a problem of the nerves, muscles, or brain that aim them: a diabetes nerve palsy, myasthenia gravis, a stroke, or an aneurysm pressing on a nerve. New double vision of the two-eye kind is an urgent evaluation; with a severe headache or a changed pupil, it is an emergency.

Nearest shelves:

Breath that smells bad (halitosis). Nine times out of ten the source is the mouth itself: bacteria coating the tongue and teeth, gum disease, a dry mouth, tonsil stones. Garlic and onions pass through in a day. The medical causes beyond the mouth: sinus infection, reflux, the sweet fruity breath of diabetic ketoacidosis, and the particular smells of kidney and liver failure. Bad breath that survives good dental care goes to the dentist first — mints cover a smell; they do not fix the gum disease making it.

Nearest shelves:

An eye that looks red. There are two common kinds. The first is pink eye (conjunctivitis): the whole surface looks pink and feels irritated — itchy or gritty, often with discharge — from a virus, bacteria, or allergies. The second kind is a burst surface blood vessel (a subconjunctival hemorrhage): a bright red patch of blood sitting on the white of the eye, often after a hard cough, a sneeze, straining, or vomiting. It looks alarming, but it does not hurt, does not affect vision, and clears on its own in a week or two, like a bruise. The dangerous kind is different: a single eye that is red and painful, with blurred vision, sensitivity to light, or a pupil that looks wrong — that can be inflammation inside the eye or acute glaucoma, and it needs same-day care. Eye drops that merely "get the red out" hide the cause, not the problem.

Nearest shelves:

A headache that is more than a headache: throbbing, usually on one side, with nausea, sensitivity to light and sound, and the wish to lie still in a dark room — attacks lasting hours to days. Some people get an aura first: flashing lights, zigzags, a blind spot, or tingling in the face or hand, for up to an hour. It is a disorder of brain signaling, not "just stress," and it has specific treatments — plain painkillers late in an attack often fail. New migraine-like headaches after age 50, or a first "worst ever" headache with a stiff neck, fever, weakness, or vision change, are not migraine until a cause is ruled out.

Nearest shelves:

The prostate gland — walnut-sized, wrapped around the urethra below the bladder — grows with age in most men, and when it does it squeezes the outflow: a weak stream, starting and stopping, feeling that the bladder never empties, frequent urination, and getting up at night. It is not cancer — benign enlargement (BPH) and prostate cancer are different conditions that can share symptoms, which is why new urinary trouble in an older man earns an examination rather than an assumption. It is manageable — medicines that relax or shrink it, and procedures when they fail.

Nearest shelves:

A swelling or firm spot in the breast that feels different from the tissue around it. Most breast lumps are not cancer — cysts, fibroadenomas (common in younger women), and areas of thickened glandular tissue are the usual explanations — and many change with the menstrual cycle. Pain is a useful guide here too: a painful lump is usually a cyst or an infection, and less likely to be cancer. The dangerous kind is the opposite — a lump that is painless and hard, as firm as your nose or firmer, and fixed in place rather than movable. A painless, hard lump should be seen by your doctor promptly, not watched. Also concerning: skin dimpling, pulling in of the nipple, bloody discharge from one nipple. Any new lump that persists past one cycle needs imaging — a mammogram and, often, an ultrasound — not watchful reassurance alone.

Nearest shelves:

Any vaginal bleeding that starts a year or more after the last period. It is never "just a late period" — after menopause, bleeding means something is bleeding: thinning and dryness of the vaginal lining (atrophy) is the commonest cause, and polyps and fibroids are on the list, but the reason every case gets checked is cancer of the lining of the womb (endometrial cancer), which most often announces itself exactly this way — and which is usually caught early because of it. The workup is an examination and an ultrasound, and often a biopsy of the lining.

Nearest shelves:

Pain in one or both testicles. The emergency is torsion: a testicle twists on its cord, cutting off its blood, and it arrives as sudden, severe pain — often in a teenager or young man, sometimes after sleep or sport — with swelling and the testicle sitting higher than usual. That is a race against the clock: the testicle is saved only if untwisted within hours. The slower causes: infection of the epididymis (often a urinary infection or, in younger men, a sexually transmitted one), a varicocele (swollen veins), trauma, and kidney stone pain that reports to the groin. Sudden severe testicle pain is an emergency — do not wait to see if it passes.

Nearest shelves:

Difficulty getting or keeping an erection firm enough for sex. It is a medical symptom before it is anything else: the usual causes are vascular disease (the same clogging of arteries that feeds heart attacks), diabetes, nerve damage, low testosterone, depression, and medicines — blood pressure drugs and antidepressants among them. That is why new erectile trouble in a middle-aged man is worth a heart-risk workup, not embarrassment: it can precede a heart attack by years. It is also treatable — medicines, vacuum devices, and, when needed, referral — and the first step is often just saying it out loud.

Nearest shelves:

A change in how the bowels behave that sticks: new constipation, new diarrhea, narrower stools, or a change in frequency that lasts weeks. Diet, travel, and medicines (opioids, iron, some diabetes drugs) explain most short changes. The ones that earn a colonoscopy: a change that persists beyond a few weeks, blood in the stool, unintentional weight loss, or the change arriving with anemia — because bowel cancer often announces itself exactly this way, quietly, through a change in habit. In anyone over 45, new persistent change is a colonoscopy question, not a fiber question.

Nearest shelves:

Pain that travels down the leg along the sciatic nerve — from the buttock, down the back of the thigh, sometimes to the foot — usually from a slipped disc pressing on a nerve root in the lower back. The pattern that marks it: pain that is worse than the back pain itself, shoots or burns in a band, and worsens with coughing or straining. Most sciatica settles over weeks with movement and time. The emergency version: weakness in the foot, numbness around the genitals or bottom ("saddle" numbness), or losing control of bladder or bowels — cauda equina syndrome, which needs an operation the same day.

Nearest shelves:

A painful, blistering rash in a band on one side of the body, caused by the chickenpox virus waking up after years asleep in a nerve. It starts with burning or tingling pain before the blisters appear, follows one nerve's territory, and doesn't cross the midline — that band is the giveaway. It is most common after 50 and when the immune system is weak. Antivirals help only if started within three days, which is why an early look matters; the pain can outlast the rash for months (postherpetic neuralgia), especially in older people. A vaccine exists and is recommended for adults 50 and over.

Nearest shelves:

Swollen veins in and around the anus and lower rectum — piles, in the older word. They come in two kinds: internal, which usually announce themselves as painless bright red bleeding on the paper or in the bowl, and external, which itch, ache, and can clot into a sudden, very tender lump. Straining, sitting long on the toilet, pregnancy, and chronic constipation feed them. Most settle with fiber, fluids, and not straining. The one rule that matters: bleeding blamed on hemorrhoids in an older person still needs the bowel checked — the hemorrhoids may be real and innocent, and something upstream may not be.

Nearest shelves:

A long-running pattern of belly pain tied to the bowels — pain that eases after a bowel movement, with diarrhea, constipation, or swings between the two, plus bloating — in a gut that looks normal on every test. It is a disorder of gut-brain communication: the bowel senses stretch too keenly and moves too fast or too slow. It does not cause bleeding, weight loss, or anemia — those findings mean look for something else. Diet (the fermentable carbohydrates — the FODMAP foods — are common triggers), stress management, and targeted medicines are the treatment; it is miserable but not dangerous.

Nearest shelves:

Periods heavy enough to run your life: soaking a pad or tampon every hour or two, passing clots the size of a quarter or bigger, bleeding past a week, or flooding through clothes or bedding. The causes: fibroids and polyps in the womb, hormone imbalance (common in the teens and again approaching menopause), a bleeding tendency, thyroid trouble, and sometimes a copper IUD. Heavy bleeding drains iron — fatigue and anemia are the quiet consequences, and iron should be checked. A change toward heavier is itself a finding, whatever the cause turns out to be.

Nearest shelves:

Cramps and pelvic pain with menstruation (dysmenorrhea). In teenagers and young women it is usually primary — the womb's own contractions, driven by prostaglandins, with nothing structurally wrong — and it responds to anti-inflammatory medicines (NSAIDs) started early. Pain that begins later in life, keeps worsening, arrives with pain at other times of the month, pain with sex, or trouble conceiving points to a cause: endometriosis above all, also fibroids and adenomyosis. Period pain that rules two or three days of every month is not something to simply endure — it deserves a workup.

Nearest shelves:

Wetting the bed during sleep (nocturnal enuresis), in a child old enough to be dry — most children are dry by five. It is common (about 1 in 10 six-year-olds), runs in families, and is no one's fault: the usual reasons are a bladder that matures slowly, deep sleep that misses the full-bladder signal, or making more urine at night. Punishment is pointless and harmful. It almost always resolves with time; alarm training is the most effective treatment when the family wants one. New bedwetting in a child who had been dry, or wetting with daytime symptoms, thirst, or weight loss, needs a check — infection and diabetes are on that list.

Nearest shelves:

Itchy, raised welts (urticaria) that appear suddenly, move around, and fade within hours, each spot gone within a day — the skin's reaction to histamine released by mast cells. Triggers: infections (the commonest, especially in children), foods, medicines, insect stings — and often no trigger is ever found. Hives alone are uncomfortable; hives with swelling of the lips or tongue, hoarseness, or trouble breathing is anaphylaxis and an emergency. Hives that keep coming for more than six weeks are called chronic, and they are usually autoimmune, not an allergy — allergy testing rarely finds the answer.

Nearest shelves:

Small, painful blisters on or around the lips (herpes labialis), caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 — caught usually in childhood, then living quietly in the nerve for life. Sunlight, fever, stress, and a cold wake it up: tingling first, then the blister cluster, crusting, and healing in a week or two. It is contagious while active — avoid kissing and sharing cups — and dangerous mainly to newborns and people with weak immune systems. Antiviral cream or tablets help most when started at the first tingle. Sores inside the mouth are usually canker sores — a different thing, not herpes, not contagious.

Nearest shelves:

Enlarged, twisted veins just under the skin, usually of the legs. The valves inside leg veins are meant to keep blood moving up against gravity; when they fail, blood pools, pressure rises, and the vein bulges. Standing for long hours, pregnancy, age, and family tendency feed them.
