Most are a cosmetic nuisance plus aching and heaviness by day's end; the complications are skin darkening and ulcers near the ankle, surface clots, and bleeding from a knocked vein. Compression stockings, walking, and leg elevation are the base treatment; procedures exist for veins that cause symptoms. A leg that swells suddenly and hurts is not varicose veins — that is a possible deep clot, same-day care.

Nearest shelves:

Numbness, tingling, and pain in the hand — thumb, index, middle finger — from the median nerve being squeezed where it passes through a tight channel at the wrist. Classic pattern: it wakes you at night, and shaking the hand helps; holding a phone, a book, or a steering wheel brings it on. Diabetes roughly doubles the chance of getting it (odds ratio about 1.7 in large studies). It is also common in pregnancy — mostly in the last three months — and usually settles after the baby comes. Repetitive wrist work raises the risk too. Left alone it can progress to constant numbness and a weak, clumsy thumb. A wrist splint at night is the first treatment; injections and a small operation to open the channel are the later ones.

Nearest shelves:

Pain in the jaw, in front of the ear, or in the chewing muscles. The usual source is the jaw joint and its muscles (temporomandibular disorder, TMD) — clicking, aching that worsens with chewing, morning soreness from grinding the teeth at night, sometimes a jaw that sticks. Dental trouble — an abscessed tooth — refers pain to the jaw too. Two causes must never be missed: jaw pain or tightness that comes with exertion and fades with rest can be angina — the heart's pain reporting to the jaw — and in an older person, jaw pain when chewing that stops when you stop, with a new headache, points to giant cell arteritis. New jaw pain with either pattern is same-day medicine, not dentistry.

Nearest shelves:

How many patients must be treated, for as long as the trial treated them, for one extra patient to benefit. It is the arithmetic flip of the absolute risk reduction: if a treatment cuts events from 10 in 100 (10%) to 7 in 100 (7%), the absolute reduction is 3 in 100 (3%) and the NNT is about 33. This is why a headline "30% reduction" needs its base rate: a 30% relative reduction on a 10% five-year risk is a 3% absolute gain — NNT about 33 over five years — while the same 30% on a 1% risk is an NNT over 300. Relative numbers advertise; the NNT tells you the workload per person helped.

Nearest shelves:

The rule that a trial analyzes every patient in the group they were randomized to, whether or not they actually took the treatment, crossed over, or dropped out. It feels unfair — counting people against a drug they never took — but it protects the one thing randomization bought: groups that differ only by chance. Drop everyone who stopped the drug and the groups quietly re-sort themselves by health, wealth, and willpower. Analyses that count only patients who completed treatment as directed (per-protocol) are shown for contrast, and when the two disagree, intention-to-treat is the one to believe for benefit.

Nearest shelves:

A trial designed to show a new treatment is not unacceptably worse than the standard one — usually because it is cheaper, safer, gentler, or easier to take. Before the trial starts, the investigators must declare the margin: the largest disadvantage they will still call acceptable — how much worse the new treatment may be than the standard and still count as "not unacceptably worse." The new treatment is declared noninferior only if the confidence interval for the difference stays inside that margin — and noninferior is not the same as equal, and not the same as better. Everything hangs on that margin — set it wide and almost anything passes — and on the analysis, which in these trials should hold up both ways of counting patients, not just the flattering one. A trial that merely fails to prove superiority has shown nothing about noninferiority; "no significant difference" is not the same as "close enough, by a margin declared in advance."

A stand-in measurement — a lab value, a scan number, a rhythm on a monitor — used in place of the outcome patients actually feel: death, heart attack, fracture, going home. Surrogates answer fast and cheap, which is why trials love them, but a treatment can move the number and miss the patient: drugs have lowered blood sugar without preventing heart attacks, and raised the "good" cholesterol without preventing anything. A surrogate earns trust only when treatments that move it have repeatedly been shown to move the real outcome too. On these shelves, hard outcomes outrank surrogates, always.

Nearest shelves:

A count of how many patients' outcomes would have to flip — one event becoming a non-event, or the reverse — to erase a trial's statistical significance. A result with a fragility index of 1 or 2 rests on one or two patients: a single transfer, a single missed follow-up, and the headline changes. Large, robust trials have fragility indices in the dozens. It is a plain-language stress test for any "P < 0.05" claim.

Nearest shelves:

A comparison of event rates between two groups, moment by moment over a trial's follow-up: a hazard ratio of 0.70 means that at any given time, the treated group is having events at 70% of the control group's rate — a 30% relative reduction in the rate. It is not the same as the difference in total risk by the end: the same hazard ratio can mean many events prevented in a high-risk group or very few in a low-risk one, which is why these shelves print the absolute rates beside it whenever the paper reports them. A confidence interval that crosses 1.0 means the data are compatible with no difference at all.

Nearest shelves:

A protein inside heart muscle cells that leaks into the blood when heart muscle is injured. It is the blood test at the center of heart-attack diagnosis: a rising or falling pattern with at least one value above the 99th percentile of healthy people, together with symptoms or ECG changes, defines a heart attack. Modern high-sensitivity tests detect tiny injuries — which cuts both ways, because troponin also rises when the heart is strained by other illness: severe infection, kidney failure, a racing rhythm, a blood clot in the lung. An elevated troponin says the heart is injured; it does not by itself say a blocked artery did it.

Nearest shelves:

A blood marker that rises mainly with bacterial infection, used — usually alongside the clinical picture, never instead of it — to help decide whether to start or stop antibiotics. Where it comes from: in health it is the precursor of the hormone calcitonin, made in the thyroid's C cells and converted on the spot, so nearly none reaches the blood. Bacterial infection changes the factory: bacterial toxin and the inflammatory signals — TNF-α and interleukin-6 — switch its gene on in tissues all over the body. The liver is the main source during infection; the spleen contributes, along with lung, kidney, fat, and gut, while lymphocytes contribute only a little. And because those tissues cannot finish converting it to calcitonin, the unfinished precursor is what pours into the blood and gets measured. In trials of patients with respiratory infections and sepsis, procalcitonin-guided care shortened antibiotic courses without worse outcomes. Its limits matter as much: it also rises after major surgery, trauma, and severe inflammation of any cause, and a low value early in an infection does not rule one out. It is a tie-breaker for antibiotics, not a sepsis detector.

Nearest shelves:

A fall in blood pressure on standing up: a drop of at least 20 points in the top number or 10 in the bottom number within three minutes of standing. Age, dehydration, diabetes, Parkinson's disease, and above all medicines — blood-pressure pills, prostate pills, antidepressants — blunt the reflex. The consequences are dizziness, falls, and fractures. It is found by measuring, not asking: blood pressure lying down, then again at one and three minutes standing. When it is found, the first treatment is often removing or timing a drug, not adding one.

Nearest shelves:

A number calculated from the routine electrolytes — sodium minus chloride and bicarbonate — that detects acids accumulating in the blood. A normal gap is roughly 8–16. A high gap has a short, serious list: lactate from shock or sepsis, ketones from diabetic ketoacidosis, kidney failure, and poisons such as methanol. A metabolic acidosis with a normal gap points elsewhere — diarrhea and kidney tubular problems head that list. One correction matters: albumin carries much of the normal gap, so in a sick patient with low albumin the gap looks deceptively small — the gap must be read against the albumin.

Nearest shelves:

Taking many medicines at once — researchers usually draw the line at five or more, though no count alone makes it wrong. Each drug on the list was usually added for a real reason; the harm lives in the pile: medicines that sedate, lower blood pressure, or block acetylcholine add up across prescribers who may never see the whole list, and the results are falls, confusion, kidney injury, and admissions. The question polypharmacy asks is not "why is this patient on so much?" but "which of these would we not start today, knowing everything we now know?"

Nearest shelves:

The planned, supervised process of tapering or stopping a medicine whose harms now outweigh its benefits, or whose benefit has simply run out — the blood-pressure pill dose from a heavier decade, the sleeping pill that outlived the crisis it was prescribed for. It is prescribing, done in reverse and with the same care: one change at a time, a watch for withdrawal or rebound, and a plan for what to do if symptoms return. Deprescribing is not abandonment; a medicine stopped deliberately, with follow-up, is treatment.

Nearest shelves:

A list, maintained by the American Geriatrics Society and updated every few years, of medicines that are potentially inappropriate in older adults — drugs where the risk commonly outweighs the benefit after 65, or that clash with diseases common in old age. It is a caution flag, not a ban — and its listings are not all based on randomized trials: most rest on observational associations and expert consensus rather than randomized trials showing harm, and a listed drug can still be the right choice for a particular patient. Its best use is as a prompt — every drug on the list should be able to explain itself on an older person's chart.

Nearest shelves:

Protein in the urine in amounts beyond the trace that is normal. The kidney's filter is meant to hold protein back, so protein leaking through is a sign the filter is injured — and a risk marker for both kidney decline and cardiovascular events. The familiar part of it is albumin (albuminuria), the protein routine testing measures — and in the commonest pattern, where the filter itself leaks (glomerular proteinuria), albumin makes up approximately 70% of the protein lost; total protein also catches other kinds, including the light chains of myeloma, which albumin-specific tests can miss. A single positive dipstick is not a diagnosis: fever, exercise, and infection cause brief leaks. Persistent proteinuria, confirmed on repeat testing and measured properly, is the finding that counts.

Nearest shelves:

Finding a real abnormality that would never have caused symptoms or death in the person's lifetime. It is screening's shadow: the slow prostate cancer in an 85-year-old, the tiny thyroid cancer that would have sat quietly forever. The diagnosis is technically correct — that is what makes it hard — but everything that follows it is pure harm: the biopsies, the surgery, the lifelong label, spent on a disease that was never going to matter. Overdiagnosis cannot be counted in any one patient; it is visible only in populations, when screening finds far more disease yet deaths from that disease barely move.

Nearest shelves:

The illusion that screening prolongs life when it has only prolonged the diagnosis. If a cancer is found three years earlier by a scan but the person dies on the same day they would have anyway, survival "from diagnosis" looks three years longer — yet nothing was gained except three extra years of knowing. Lead-time bias is why survival statistics flatter screening programs, and why the only honest test of screening is whether fewer people die of the disease (and of everything) in a randomized comparison — not how long the diagnosed live after the label.

Nearest shelves:

The fact that in real patients, especially older ones, something else may happen first. A treatment aimed at preventing a heart attack in ten years competes with the cancers, infections, and frailty that may intervene in three; a patient who dies of pneumonia cannot go on to have the stroke the trial was counting. When analyses ignore competing risks, they overstate how much of the target outcome is actually available to be prevented — and overstate the treatment's value in exactly the oldest, sickest patients where the question matters most.

Nearest shelves:

A comparison of odds rather than probabilities: the odds of an outcome in one group divided by the odds in another. When an outcome is rare, the odds ratio is close to the relative risk and can be read almost the same way. When the outcome is common, it exaggerates: a risk that rises from 25 in 100 (25%) to 40 in 100 (40%) is a relative risk of 1.6, but an odds ratio of 2.0. Case-control studies can only produce odds ratios, which is one more reason their big numbers deserve a discount until confirmed in trials.

Nearest shelves:

The two halves of a test's accuracy. Sensitivity is the share of people who truly have the condition that the test catches — a sensitivity of 90% means it misses 1 in 10 cases. Specificity is the share of people who truly do not have it that the test clears — a specificity of 90% means it falsely alarms 1 in 10 healthy people. Neither number tells you what a positive result means for the patient in front of you: that depends on how common the condition is in people like them, which is why a good test used on the wrong population produces mostly false alarms. In one sentence: sensitivity is how many of the truly sick the test catches, and specificity is how many of the truly well it clears.

Nearest shelves:

The statistical gravity that pulls an extreme measurement toward average on the next reading. Blood pressure caught at a painful, rushed moment will usually be lower when rechecked calmly; the worst week of pain is likely to be followed by a better one, whatever you prescribe. Regression to the mean is the great mimic of treatment effects: start any remedy at the worst moment and it will look like it works. It is why careful medicine repeats the measurement before acting on it, and why trials need a control group — the control group is where regression to the mean shows itself honestly.

Nearest shelves:

The harm-side twin of the number needed to treat: how many patients must receive a treatment, for as long as the trial gave it, for one extra patient to be harmed. If a drug causes a serious side effect in 2 in 100 (2%) against 1 in 100 (1%) on placebo, the absolute increase is 1 in 100 (1%) and the NNH is 100. A treatment is only worth taking when its benefit and harm are weighed on the same scale: an NNT of 33 to prevent one event against an NNH of 100 for a milder harm is one judgment; the same NNT against an NNH of 40 for a worse harm is another. Any benefit claim quoted without its NNH is half a sentence.

Nearest shelves:

The plain subtraction at the heart of every honest benefit claim: the event rate without treatment minus the event rate with it. A fall from 10 in 100 (10%) to 7 in 100 (7%) is an absolute risk reduction of 3 in 100 (3 percentage points) — no matter that the same result can be dressed as a 30% relative reduction. Absolute reduction is the number a patient actually experiences, the number the number-needed-to-treat is built from, and the only form in which benefits can be compared across treatments, trials, and base rates. These shelves label relative figures as relative and print absolute rates beside them whenever the paper reports them.

Nearest shelves:

An analysis that counts only the patients who actually completed the trial as directed — took the drug, stayed in their assigned group, finished follow-up. It answers a tidy question (what does the treatment do in people who truly receive it?) and a biased one, because the patients who stick with a treatment differ from those who stop it — healthier, hardier, fewer side effects — in ways no adjustment fully repairs. When per-protocol and intention-to-treat disagree about benefit, intention-to-treat is the one to believe; per-protocol earns its keep mainly in noninferiority trials and in counting harms among the actually exposed.

Nearest shelves:

Hiding who got which treatment from the people who could be swayed by knowing. A double-blind trial keeps both patients and their treating clinicians in the dark; the strongest designs also blind the people who judge the outcomes. Blinding matters most where judgment is softest — pain, function, "clinical improvement," decisions to hospitalize — and least where the outcome is a hard count like death. A blind can also quietly break: a drug with an unmistakable side effect unblinds itself, which is why well-run trials sometimes ask participants to guess their group at the end.

Nearest shelves:

The range of values a study's result is compatible with. A hazard ratio of 0.70 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.55 to 0.89 says the data comfortably include everything from a large benefit to a modest one; the same 0.70 with an interval of 0.39 to 1.09 reaches past 1.0 — no difference at all — and the honest reading changes from "works" to "might work." Width is the message: narrow intervals come from many events and mean precision; wide ones come from small trials and mean the study has narrowed the truth down to a neighborhood, not an address. Read the interval, not just the headline number inside it.

Nearest shelves:

Of all the people a test calls positive, the share who truly have the condition. It is where sensitivity and specificity meet real life, because it depends on how common the condition is in the people tested: screen a population where 1 in 1,000 has the disease with a test that is 99% specific, and most positives are false alarms; test people already likely to have it, and the same test's positives are usually real. A positive result is a probability, not a verdict, and this is the number that says how big.

Nearest shelves:

A chemical the body produces when cells burn glucose without enough oxygen — the exhaust of emergency energy production — and a blood level that rises in shock and sepsis, where it marks tissues being under-perfused and predicts death better than blood pressure does. It is not specific to infection or low oxygen: hard seizures, vigorous exercise, asthma medicines like albuterol, and a tourniquet left on during the blood draw all raise it. What matters clinically is the level and its direction — a lactate that falls as treatment proceeds is the circulation recovering; one that climbs is the opposite.

Nearest shelves:

The yellow pigment left when old red blood cells are broken down and their hemoglobin is dismantled. The liver processes it and excretes it into bile; when it accumulates — from blood breaking down too fast, a liver too sick to process it, or a bile duct blocked downstream — it stains the skin and eyes yellow (jaundice). The pattern of the rest of the liver tests usually separates the three causes. Newborns commonly run high for a few days while their livers mature, which is why nurseries watch the level and use light therapy to bring it down.

Nearest shelves:

A bedside score of consciousness built from three responses: eye opening (scored 1–4), speech (1–5), and movement (1–6), summed from 3 (deep coma) to 15 (fully alert). It gives every clinician the same shorthand for a brain's state and its direction — a falling score after head injury is an emergency in one number. Its limits are practical: a breathing tube removes speech, sedation and paralysis flatten everything, and alcohol imitates injury. The components matter as much as the total — two patients at 8 got there by different roads — which is why careful teams report the parts, not just the sum.

Nearest shelves:

Removing the breathing tube from a patient who has been on a ventilator. The judgment is a balance of two harms: leave the tube and each extra day brings infection, sedation, and weakness; pull it too soon and the patient who cannot protect their airway or sustain the work of breathing fails — and needing the tube reinserted (reintubation) carries its own real risk of death. Readiness is tested, not guessed: awake enough to protect the airway, strong enough cough, and a supervised trial of breathing on minimal support, watched closely, before the tube comes out.

Nearest shelves:

The rate at which new cases of a condition appear in a population over a stated time: so many new cases per 1,000 (or 100,000) people per year. Incidence measures risk — the chance of joining the group — and it is the number prevention acts on. It is easily confused with prevalence, and the difference matters: a short, common illness (a cold) has high incidence and low prevalence, while a lifelong, well-managed one (type 2 diabetes) accumulates — modest yearly incidence, very high prevalence, because everyone who joins stays.

Nearest shelves:

The share of a population living with a condition at a given moment, usually as a percentage. Prevalence is incidence times duration: conditions people live with for decades pile up, so prevalence can be high even when the yearly risk of developing the condition is small. It is the number planners need (how many clinic visits, how much insulin) and the number that decides what a positive test means — the same test finds mostly true cases where prevalence is high and mostly false alarms where it is low.

Nearest shelves:

A measure of how surprising a study's data would be if the treatment truly did nothing. A p value of 0.03 means: in a world where the treatment is useless, results at least this extreme would still show up about 3 times in 100 (3%) by chance alone. Two misunderstandings follow it everywhere: it is NOT the probability that the result is true (nor that it is false), and crossing the conventional 0.05 line says nothing about whether an effect is big enough to matter. Read it as a rough gauge of how hard the data argue against "nothing happening" — then read the confidence interval and the absolute numbers to find out what is actually happening.

Nearest shelves:

A positive test result in a person who does not have the condition. False positives are not laboratory errors; they are arithmetic. A test with 99% specificity falsely alarms 1 in 100 (1%) of healthy people tested — screen 10,000 healthy people and roughly 100 will be told something may be wrong, each owed a workup of scans, biopsies, and anxious weeks. When the condition is rare, false positives can outnumber true ones many times over, which is why screening programs are judged on the whole cascade they start, not only the cancers they catch.

Nearest shelves:

The smallest change in an outcome that patients themselves perceive as worthwhile — the least improvement in pain, breathlessness, or function that a person would say justified the trouble of treatment. It is the yardstick statistical significance lacks: a large trial can make a change of almost nothing statistically significant, while a result can miss significance in a small trial yet exceed what patients would call meaningful. When a paper reports a benefit, the question to ask of it is not only "is it real?" but "would anyone feel it?"

Nearest shelves:

A trial design in which every participant receives each treatment in turn — drug first, then placebo, or the reverse — separated by a washout period, so each person serves as their own control. It is efficient: differences between people, the great noise of parallel trials, cancel out, and far fewer participants are needed. It only works when the condition is stable over time and the first treatment leaves nothing behind — no cure, no lasting change, no learning — which is why crossover designs suit chronic symptoms (pain, reflux, blood pressure) and fail for surgery, vaccines, and anything meant to change the disease itself.

Nearest shelves:

A written statement of the care a person would want if they could no longer speak for themselves. It usually has two parts: a living will, naming the treatments they would accept or refuse in stated situations, and a health care proxy (or durable power of attorney for health care), naming the person trusted to decide. A directive guides; it is not itself a medical order — the actionable bedside version is a POLST/MOLST form, signed by a clinician. The document only works if it can be found and if the named person knows it exists: a directive in a drawer is a wish, not a plan.

Nearest shelves:

A model of care for the last phase of life, when the goal shifts from prolonging life to protecting its quality: expert control of pain and breathlessness, support for the family, and a team — nurse, aide, social worker, chaplain, physician — usually delivered at home. Under the US Medicare benefit it is for people whose doctors judge the prognosis to be six months or less if the illness runs its course; choosing it means leaving behind treatments aimed at cure, not leaving behind care. Its persistent tragedy is timing: many patients are referred only in the final days, when there is little time left for hospice to do what it is good at.

Nearest shelves:

Specialized care aimed at relief — of pain, breathlessness, nausea, fear — for people living with serious illness, at any stage and alongside curative treatment. Unlike hospice, it requires no prognosis and no giving up of anything: the same team that helps a patient through chemotherapy helps them decide, over time, what treatment is still worth its burden. Trials of early palliative care in advanced cancer found better quality of life and mood, and in one landmark trial, longer survival. It is the part of medicine that treats the person carrying the disease, and it is underused mostly because it is mistaken for end-of-life care alone.

A tube passed through the abdominal wall into the stomach (placed endoscopically, it is a PEG) so liquid nutrition can be given when swallowing is impossible or unsafe — after some strokes, in diseases of the swallowing muscles, or when the gut must be fed during a long recovery. It bypasses the mouth, not the lungs: food and saliva can still be inhaled, so a feeding tube does not reliably prevent aspiration pneumonia, the harm it is most often placed to avoid. In advanced dementia, guidelines recommend careful hand feeding as tolerated instead — tubes there have not been shown to prolong life or prevent aspiration, and they add restraint, infection, and hospital transfers to a life already narrowing.

Nearest shelves:

The risk of an outcome in one group divided by the risk in another. If events occur in 7 in 100 (7%) of treated patients and 10 in 100 (10%) of controls, the relative risk is 0.70 — a 30% relative risk reduction. That same result is an absolute reduction of 3 in 100 (3 percentage points), and relative risk alone never tells you which of those you are looking at: a relative risk of 0.70 on a common outcome prevents many events, and on a rare one almost none. Relative risk also says nothing by itself about whether a difference is real or chance — that is the confidence interval's job. On these shelves a percent drawn from a relative measure is always labeled relative, and the absolute rates are printed beside it whenever the paper reports them.

Nearest shelves:

A trial outcome built by pooling several different events into one count — classically death, heart attack, and stroke pooled as "major adverse cardiovascular events." That classic three-part pool has a name of its own: MACE — major adverse cardiovascular events — meaning cardiovascular death, nonfatal heart attack, and nonfatal stroke counted together as one outcome. Some trials widen it to four or five parts by adding hospitalization for unstable angina or a repeat procedure to open a blocked artery (revascularization), so whenever a card reports MACE it says which parts were counted. Pooling buys events, and events buy statistical power, which is why large trials use composites. The cost is honesty about what moved: the components are rarely equal in importance, and the composite is often driven by its commonest, softest member — hospitalizations or repeat procedures — while death, the component patients care about most, barely changes. The rule for reading one: never accept the pooled number until you have seen each component separately and found which one did the work.

Nearest shelves:

Re-examining a trial's result inside slices of its patients — older or younger, men or women, sicker or less sick. Subgroups feel informative and are mostly a trap: test enough slices and chance guarantees a winner — run 20 subgroups at the usual significance line and about one will look positive even if the treatment does nothing differently in anyone. The landmark warning came from the ISIS-2 aspirin trial, whose investigators showed that aspirin appeared not to work in patients born under Gemini or Libra — a result nobody believed, published precisely to show what slicing can manufacture. A subgroup claim earns belief only when it was declared in advance, is one of very few tested, is large, and survives the honest test — comparing the subgroups against each other (an interaction test) — rather than merely being significant in one slice and not the other.

Nearest shelves:

A planned gap with no treatment, used before a trial starts or between the two halves of a crossover trial, so the previous drug's effect clears before the next measurement. It only works if it is long enough: a drug's effect fades with its half-life, and after about five half-lives roughly 97% is gone. Too short a washout lets the first treatment leak into the second period (carryover) and quietly corrupts the comparison. Washouts also have limits in the other direction — a needed treatment cannot always be paused safely, and a treatment that cures or permanently changes the disease can never be washed out at all.

Nearest shelves:

A negative test result in a person who does have the condition — the missing twin of the false positive. False negatives are arithmetic, not laboratory errors: a test with 90% sensitivity misses 10 in 100 (10%) of true cases, so whether a negative result should reassure you depends on how likely the condition was before the test. Early in an infection, before the marker rises, is the classic setup. When suspicion stays high after a negative result, the correct move is not to accept the verdict but to repeat the test, use a different one, or treat the patient in front of you — a negative result lowers a probability; it rarely erases one.

Nearest shelves:

The step-shaped graph trials use to show survival — or freedom from any event — over time. The line starts at 100% and steps down each time an event occurs; small tick marks show censoring, the patients who left the picture alive or uncounted (study ended, lost to follow-up). Reading one well means three habits: watch where the two groups' curves separate and whether they stay separated or cross; distrust the far right-hand tail, where few patients remain — the little table of "numbers at risk" printed under most curves tells you how few; and remember the curve shows the share affected, not how much longer any one person lived.

Nearest shelves:

A protein made by the liver and poured into the blood whenever tissue is injured or infected. The order to make it comes mainly from interleukin-6, one of the body's central inflammatory signals; levels rise within hours, peak at about two days, and fall quickly when the cause settles. CRP is a smoke alarm, not an address: it rises with bacterial infection, heart attack, surgery, arthritis flares, and cancer alike, so a high value says "inflammation, somewhere, of roughly this size" and nothing more specific. Measured with a high-sensitivity assay (hsCRP), the low levels seen in quiet, chronic inflammation also track cardiovascular risk. Albumin moves the opposite way in the same illnesses — it falls with inflammation or injury, and diet does not lower it — which is why a low albumin is a marker of inflammation, not of what a patient eats.

Nearest shelves:

A hormone released by the heart's main pumping chambers when their walls are stretched — by pressure or by extra volume, as in heart failure. The blood tests (BNP itself, or its longer-lived companion piece NT-proBNP) earn their keep in the breathless patient: a low value makes heart failure an unlikely cause, while a high value supports it. The traps run both ways: levels also climb with age, kidney failure, and atrial fibrillation, and run deceptively lower in obesity. The name is the job description — natriuretic means promoting sodium loss into the urine, the heart's own attempt to unload the fluid that is stretching it.

Nearest shelves:

A fragment left behind when a blood clot is broken down — proof that clot was formed and dissolved somewhere in the body. Its clinical value is almost entirely in the negative: in a patient whose chance of a deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism is low or middling, a normal D-dimer makes the clot unlikely enough to stop the hunt without a scan. A raised D-dimer, by contrast, proves almost nothing on its own — surgery, pregnancy, cancer, infection, injury, and plain advancing age all raise it. Because age raises it, many emergency departments adjust the cut-off upward in patients over 50 (the patient's age times ten, in the usual units) rather than calling every older patient's result positive.

Nearest shelves:

Fluid collected in the thin space between the lung and the chest wall. A little fluid there is normal lubrication; a collection large enough to name compresses the lung and causes breathlessness, worst lying flat. The causes sort into two families: fluid pushed out by pressure or low protein — heart failure above all, also liver and kidney failure — and fluid leaked by local disease — pneumonia, cancer, a blood clot in the lung. Separating the two families is the first diagnostic job, done by sampling the fluid with a needle (thoracentesis) and comparing its protein and enzyme levels against the blood's; removing a larger volume is also the fastest relief for the breathlessness.

Nearest shelves:

The delayed benefit of good control early: in the UKPDS follow-up, the advantages of intensive glucose control (fewer heart attacks and deaths) appeared only years after the trial ended, long after glucose levels in the two groups had become the same. Sometimes called metabolic memory.

A trial design in which doses in every group are adjusted toward the same pre-set target (for example, a fasting glucose range). The comparison is then between the treatments themselves, fairly dosed — the price is that the design can hide differences in dose needed or in side effects on the way to the target.

Laser treatment for proliferative diabetic retinopathy: hundreds of small burns scattered across the peripheral retina reduce the drive to grow fragile new blood vessels. It protects the central vision the patient reads with, at the cost of some peripheral and night vision.

Treatment with drugs that block vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), the signal that makes abnormal blood vessels grow and leak. In diabetic eye disease the drug (for example ranibizumab or aflibercept) is injected into the eye to treat macular edema and proliferative retinopathy.

A newborn whose birthweight falls below the 10th percentile for babies born at the same gestational age. It is a size description, not a diagnosis: some babies are small and healthy, others are small because growth was restricted.

A newborn whose birthweight falls above the 90th percentile for babies born at the same gestational age. In diabetes in pregnancy it usually reflects the baby's exposure to extra glucose — and a higher chance of birth injury and of needing a caesarean birth.

High blood glucose with ketones present in the blood or urine, short of full diabetic ketoacidosis. Trials report it as a safety signal because ketosis is the first step on that road — the term is deliberately weaker than "ketoacidosis" and the two should not be interchanged.

A low-blood-glucose episode severe enough that the person needs another person's help to recover. Trials count it separately from milder lows the person treats themselves, because it is the level of hypoglycemia that injures, hospitalizes, and kills.
A comparison of event rates between two groups, counting repeat events per unit of time; unlike a risk ratio it uses events per person-year, so one person can contribute more than one event.

The percentage of the day a continuous glucose monitor reads in the target range of 70 to 180 mg/dL. The usual goal for most adults with diabetes is more than 70% of the day in range; time below range matters as much as time above it, because it counts the lows.

A progressive brain disease and the commonest cause of dementia: amyloid plaques and tau tangles accumulate, memory and thinking erode over years, and daily function is gradually lost. Diagnosis is clinical, increasingly supported by amyloid and tau tests; whether removing amyloid produces benefit patients can feel is a trial question — see the shelves.

A small flap-like opening between the heart's upper chambers that fails to seal shut after birth — present in about a quarter of adults. It usually causes no trouble, but a clot crossing it can reach the brain and cause a stroke; whether closing it after such a stroke helps is a trial question — see the shelves.

Narrowing of a carotid artery in the neck, usually by cholesterol plaque. It can cause a stroke when plaque ruptures or a clot forms and travels to the brain; many narrowings are found before any symptom. How best to treat it — surgery, stenting, or medicines alone — is a trial question — see the shelves.

A condition in which stomach acid repeatedly flows back into the esophagus, causing heartburn and regurgitation and sometimes damaging the esophageal lining over time. Treatment ranges from acid-suppressing medicines to antireflux surgery — see the shelves.

A group of short-chain carbohydrates — fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides and polyols — found in many fruits, vegetables, grains, dairy foods and sweeteners. They are poorly absorbed and fermented by gut bacteria, so they can provoke bloating and pain in irritable bowel syndrome; a low-FODMAP diet restricts them for a trial period.

A collection of blood between the brain's surface and its outer covering (the dura), usually from torn bridging veins. The chronic form builds up slowly over weeks, mostly in older adults, and can return after surgical drainage.
A blood-test pattern, not a symptom: the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level is raised while the thyroid hormone level (free T4) stays in the normal range. Most people with it feel no different.

A planned, monitored pause in a long-term medicine, used when a drug's benefits outlast its dosing — as bisphosphonates do, lingering in bone for years — so a pause may keep most of the benefit while shedding the risks of indefinite use.

A class of cancer drugs that block poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase, an enzyme cancer cells use to repair DNA damage. They work hardest against cancers whose other repair system is already broken — tumors with BRCA mutations or homologous recombination deficiency — which is why their benefit follows the biomarker. Olaparib and niraparib are examples, used mainly as maintenance therapy in ovarian cancer.

A tumor's inability to repair double-strand DNA breaks by the high-fidelity homologous-recombination pathway — caused by BRCA1/2 mutations or other defects in that machinery. A cancer with HRD is vulnerable to PARP inhibitors, which block its backup repair route; a cancer without it (HR-proficient) is much less so. Trials report results split by HRD status because the treatment effect splits there too.

Fever during the period when chemotherapy has driven the neutrophil count (the white cells that fight bacterial infection) dangerously low. It is treated as an emergency — blood cultures and immediate antibiotics — because in a neutropenic patient fever may be the only sign of a bloodstream infection. Chemotherapy regimens are graded by how often they cause it, and preventive G-CSF is standard when that risk reaches about 20%.

Treatment that stops the body making testosterone, or blocks its action, used against prostate cancer, whose growth testosterone feeds. Given with radiation for higher-risk localized disease, its benefit grows with duration up to a point — and so do its costs: hot flushes, lost libido and bone, metabolic change, and worse quality of life, which is why how long it should run is itself a trial question.

Long-standing inflammation of the nose and sinuses with soft, painless growths (polyps) in the nasal passages, causing blockage, discharge, facial pressure, and loss of smell. Ordinary disease is managed with intranasal steroids and sometimes surgery; the biologic drugs are reserved for severe disease that keeps returning despite them.

A treatment for food allergy in which the patient eats a tiny, precisely measured dose of the allergen every day, increasing slowly to a maintenance dose, in order to raise the amount that can be eaten accidentally without a reaction (desensitization). It is not a cure: protection lasts only while dosing continues for most patients, and the doses themselves commonly cause allergic reactions — the central trade-off its trials measure.

The standard score for psoriasis severity, combining how much of the body is covered with how red, thick, and scaly the plaques are. Trials report the share of patients reaching PASI-75, PASI-90, or PASI-100 — improvements of at least 75%, 90%, or a full 100% (completely clear skin). Modern biologics are compared mainly on PASI-90.

A rapid loss of hearing (typically at least 30 dB over three frequencies within 72 hours) from the inner ear or hearing nerve, usually in one ear and usually without an identifiable cause. It is treated as an emergency because the window for any treatment to help is short, and a substantial share of cases recover partly or fully on their own — which is what makes its treatment evidence hard to read.

Treatment of an allergy by giving the patient the allergen itself in controlled, gradually sufficient doses (under the tongue — SLIT — or by injection) over years, to retrain the immune response rather than merely block symptoms. It is the only allergy treatment whose benefit can persist after it stops; whether it can prevent asthma from developing is a separate, unproven claim.

An autoimmune condition in which the skin's pigment cells (melanocytes) are destroyed, leaving smooth white patches, often on the face and hands. It is not contagious and does not damage internal organs, but its visibility makes it heavily burdensome. Repigmentation, when treatment works at all, is slow and usually partial.

A chronic inflammatory skin disease of hair follicles in the armpits, groin, and similar areas, causing painful boils and abscesses that can join into draining tunnels and leave rope-like scars. Despite the name it is not primarily an infection. Trials grade response with HiSCR: at least a 50% fall in abscess and inflammatory-nodule count with no new abscesses or draining fistulas.

Inflammation of large and medium arteries, almost always in people over 50, classically causing new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when chewing, and — its emergency — sudden vision loss from an inflamed artery to the eye. Treatment is immediate high-dose glucocorticoids, then a long, toxic taper that modern biologic therapy tries to shorten.

A group of diseases (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and renal-limited vasculitis) in which autoantibodies called ANCA drive inflammation of small blood vessels, attacking especially the kidneys and lungs. Untreated it was usually fatal; remission is induced with cyclophosphamide or rituximab plus glucocorticoids, then held with maintenance treatment.

A treatment for food allergy in which the allergic person swallows tiny, gradually increasing amounts of the food under medical supervision, raising the dose that triggers a reaction while treatment continues (desensitization). The protection usually fades if dosing stops; it is not the same as outgrowing the allergy.

In food-allergy immunotherapy, still passing a food challenge after a period of eating none of the food and taking no treatment — a step beyond desensitization, which is tested while still dosing, but short of proven lifelong tolerance.

A chronic allergic inflammation of the esophagus (food pipe) in which eosinophils — a type of white blood cell — build up in its lining, causing difficulty swallowing and food getting stuck. It is diagnosed by biopsy at endoscopy; the trial threshold for histologic remission is no more than 6 eosinophils per high-power microscope field.

An inherited deficiency or dysfunction of the C1 inhibitor protein that lets the kallikrein–bradykinin pathway trigger episodes of deep swelling of the skin, gut, or airway — without hives, and unresponsive to antihistamines or epinephrine. Airway attacks can be fatal; modern prophylaxis blocks plasma kallikrein or replaces C1 inhibitor.

Raised, itchy welts on the skin. Chronic spontaneous urticaria means hives on most days for more than six weeks with no external trigger found — the immune system activates the skin’s mast cells on its own. Trials score it with the UAS7: itch plus hives over seven days, where 0 is complete response.

A pattern of opioid use that causes significant impairment or distress — craving, loss of control over use, and continued use despite harm. It is treated with medicines (methadone, buprenorphine, naltrexone) that reduce craving and relapse; how well each works is a trial question — see the shelves.

A medicine that rapidly reverses an opioid overdose by blocking opioid receptors, restoring breathing within minutes. It is given by injection or nasal spray, is safe in people who are not overdosing, and wears off within an hour or so — which is why emergency services should still be called.

A behavioral treatment that gives tangible rewards — vouchers or prizes — for verified target behavior, most often a drug-negative urine test. The rewards are the treatment; what happens when they stop is a separate question the shelves grade separately.

Major depression that has not responded adequately to at least two antidepressant treatments in the current episode. It is the population studied in the esketamine, ketamine, and psilocybin trials on the shelves — results there do not automatically extend to depression that has not yet had standard treatment.

A pregnancy complication of high blood pressure with signs of organ strain — protein in the urine, or effects on the liver, kidneys, blood, or brain — arising after 20 weeks. The preterm form (delivered before 37 weeks) is the dangerous early disease the aspirin trials aim to prevent; the term form is a separate, milder-on-average condition, and treatments that prevent one have not been shown to prevent the other.

A group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by injury to the developing brain, most often around the time of preterm birth. It does not worsen over time, but its effects on walking, movement, and independence are lifelong — which is why preventing it, rather than treating it, is the goal of the magnesium trials.

Birth before 37 completed weeks of pregnancy. The earlier the birth, the higher the risks of death and disability: most of the trials on the pregnancy shelves enroll the earliest groups — before 34 weeks (late preterm is 34–36 weeks) or before 30 weeks — and their results do not automatically extend across the whole range.

A serious intestinal disease of newborns, mostly preterm, in which part of the bowel wall becomes inflamed and can die, sometimes perforating. It is one of the most feared complications of prematurity, and on the ORACLE shelf it is the harm that rules co-amoxiclav out after ruptured membranes.

The chronic lung disease of prematurity: lungs injured and interrupted in development by the very support that keeps an extremely preterm baby alive — oxygen and mechanical ventilation — so the baby still needs oxygen around the date they were due to be born (36 weeks). It is the “BPD” half of the “death or BPD” outcome the CPAP trials were built around.

Newborn care built on prolonged skin-to-skin contact between a low-birth-weight baby and the mother (or another caregiver), usually with frequent breastfeeding. Started after stabilization it was already standard in many units; the iKMC trial tested starting it immediately, in a unit where mothers stay resident — a median 17 hours a day of contact.

Heavy bleeding after birth, conventionally defined as blood loss of 500 mL or more after vaginal birth, with 1,000 mL or more classed as severe. It is the leading cause of maternal death worldwide, and the two thresholds are not interchangeable — a treatment can reduce moderate hemorrhage without reducing severe hemorrhage, and the shelves grade them separately.

Transfusing blood on the scale of a patient’s whole blood volume — conventionally ten or more units of red cells in 24 hours, though in practice the term means the emergency protocol itself: red cells, plasma and platelets released together, in set ratios, before laboratory results can steer.

A blood product made by thawing frozen plasma partway: the cold-insoluble fraction that settles out is rich in fibrinogen, the protein blood needs to form the mesh of a clot. It is the traditional way to replace fibrinogen in a bleeding patient.

Bedside tests that watch a small sample of blood clot in a cup and draw its strength over time as a trace — thromboelastography (TEG) and rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) are the two systems. The trace shows how fast the clot starts, how strong it gets, and whether it is breaking down, and is used to choose blood products during major bleeding.

Blood transfused as one product — red cells, plasma and platelets together in the bag, as it left the donor — instead of separated components given from different bags. Modern trauma practice mostly uses cold-stored low-titer group O whole blood.

Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta: a catheter threaded from the groin into the aorta, where a balloon is inflated to stop blood flowing past it — a clamp from inside the vessel, used to slow bleeding below the balloon until surgery can control it.

A purified fibrinogen product made from pooled human plasma, stored as a powder and reconstituted at the bedside in minutes — no thawing and no blood-group matching. It is the manufactured alternative to cryoprecipitate for replacing fibrinogen in a bleeding patient.

Assigning patients to treatment groups by chance — a coin flip, in modern dress a computer's random sequence — rather than by anyone's choice. It is the single most important design feature in this library, because it is the only method that balances the groups on factors nobody measured or even knows about: doctors choosing who gets the new drug will, however honestly, steer it toward patients they judge more (or less) likely to benefit, and no statistical adjustment fully undoes that steering. Randomization only works if the sequence is concealed until the patient is in (allocation concealment) — a predictable sequence is a choice wearing a costume. When a card here says "observational," this is the ingredient that is missing, and it is why such cards carry weaker grades.

Nearest shelves:

The middle value: half the patients fall below it, half above. Trials report medians for skewed quantities — blood loss, length of stay, time to treatment — because a few extreme values drag an average (mean) far from the typical patient: one patient who stays 90 days makes a ward's mean stay meaningless, while the median stay barely moves. The median's blind spot is the tails: two groups can share a median blood loss while one has far more catastrophic bleeds. When a card gives a median without a spread, treat the number as half a result.

Nearest shelves:

The spread printed beside a median: the range from the 25th percentile to the 75th — the middle half of patients. A median time to treatment of 29 minutes with an IQR of 23–40 means a quarter of patients were treated within 23 minutes and a quarter waited beyond 40. Read the IQR before the median: a tight IQR says the typical experience really was typical; a wide one says the headline number hides patients at both extremes, and the extremes are often where the harm or the benefit lives.

Nearest shelves:

A planned look at a trial's results while it is still running, at a pre-set point — half the patients enrolled, say, or half the expected events counted. Trials plan these looks because continuing to randomize patients after the answer is already clear (in either direction) is unethical, and because a hopeless trial wastes everyone still enrolling. The price is discipline: each peek spends some of the trial's statistical allowance, so the final result must clear a slightly higher bar, and unplanned peeking inflates false positives exactly the way subgroup slicing does. When a card says a trial "stopped at a planned interim analysis," the look was part of the design — when it just says "stopped early," ask whose look it was.

Nearest shelves:

The judgment, usually at an interim analysis, that a trial cannot succeed even if it runs to completion: the remaining patients, even if every one of them broke the treatment's way, could not push the result across the line. The formal version is conditional power — the probability of a positive final result given the data so far — and trials commonly stop when it falls below about 20–25%. A futility stop is not a finding of harm and not proof the treatment does nothing; it is proof that the effect, if any, is smaller than the trial was built to detect. Several cards distinguish the two carefully: COMBAT and FiiRST-2 stopped for futility; COCA stopped over concern about harm — different doors out of a trial, with different meanings.

Nearest shelves:

The independent committee — clinicians and statisticians with no stake in the trial — that alone sees the unblinded interim results while a trial runs. Its job is the participants, not the publication: it can recommend stopping for clear benefit (as in the kangaroo-care trial on these shelves), for harm, or for futility, and its members are the only people allowed to know which way the data are leaning while enrollment continues. A DSMB recommendation is advice to the trial's steering committee, which occasionally disagrees — when a card reports who stopped a trial and why, that chain of decision is part of the evidence.

Nearest shelves:

The honest way to ask whether a treatment works differently in one kind of patient than another: a statistical test of whether the effect in subgroup A differs from the effect in subgroup B. It exists because the common shortcut is a fallacy — "significant in men, not significant in women" does not show the treatment differs by sex; it usually shows only that one subgroup was smaller. A real difference requires the interaction test itself to be significant, and even then it earns belief only if the subgroup was named in advance and few were tested. Cards on these shelves report interaction P values where the paper gives them (for example, dialysis vs non-dialysis patients in SHARP, P=0.25 — no demonstrated difference) precisely so the reader is not left comparing significance labels.

Nearest shelves:

A study of studies: a search for every trial (or study) answering one question, run to a written protocol — databases, dates, inclusion rules declared in advance — followed by an explicit appraisal of each study's quality. Its pooled form is the meta-analysis. The protocol is what separates a systematic review from a narrative one: a reviewer free to choose studies after seeing their results can manufacture any conclusion the literature's noise permits. This library cards systematic reviews as context and synthesis, not as exhibits — a pool is only as honest as the trials inside it, and the trials are carded on their own shelves where they can be.

Nearest shelves:

The honest uncertainty that makes a randomized trial ethical: the expert community genuinely does not know which of the compared treatments is better, so offering a patient a coin flip between them wrongs no one. Equipoise is what new evidence erodes — once a trial answers the question, randomizing the next patient to the losing arm becomes hard to defend, which is one reason practice-changing trials close questions quickly. Its absence is also diagnostic: when clinicians are sure a treatment works and refuse to randomize, the "evidence" that accumulates is observational forever — several shelves here (whole blood among them) sit at weak grades for exactly that reason.

Nearest shelves:

Death from loss of blood — bleeding out. It is the mechanism, not just the outcome: a patient can receive twenty units of blood and still die of exsanguination if the bleeding outruns the replacement. In trauma it is one of the few immediately preventable causes of death, which is why the hemorrhage shelves distinguish it from all-cause mortality: in PROPPR, overall mortality did not differ significantly between transfusion ratios, but deaths from exsanguination did (9.2% vs 14.6%) — a signal visible only because the trial counted the mechanism separately. When a card reports "death due to bleeding," this is the event being counted.

Nearest shelves:

The share of colonoscopies in which at least one adenoma — a precancerous polyp — is found. It is colonoscopy's main quality score: endoscopists with higher rates miss fewer cancers in their patients later. A detection aid can raise the rate mainly by finding more tiny adenomas, which is why this library separates the detection gain from the unproven cancer gain.

A single number summarizing the small inherited risks carried at many places across the genome at once — thousands to millions of common variants, each trivial alone, added into one score. The top few percent of a score can carry risk comparable to a single-gene mutation; for most people the score moves prediction only slightly beyond ordinary clinical risk factors.

A blood test that looks for cancer signals — typically fragments of tumor DNA shed into the blood, read by their methylation pattern — across many cancer types at once, from a single draw. A positive result starts a diagnostic hunt; it is not a diagnosis, and in the first large prospective study most positive results proved to be false alarms.

Hospital-level care — daily clinician visits, intravenous medicines, monitoring — delivered in the patient's own home instead of a ward, either avoiding an admission or replacing its later days. Trials test it in selected patients who have a home, support, and an illness expected to behave; the results do not automatically extend beyond that fence.

A fixed combination of two antibiotics, trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole, that block bacterial folate production at two successive steps. Taken daily in small doses it prevents opportunistic infections — bacterial pneumonias above all — in people whose immune systems are suppressed, which is why a Zambian trial could test whether it saves children's lives even where bacteria are widely resistant to it.

The first widely used cholesterol-lowering drug of the fibrate class, taken as a daily capsule. Its 1978 WHO trial — run in Edinburgh, Budapest, and Prague — lowered cholesterol and non-fatal heart attacks while raising overall mortality during treatment, making it the founding cautionary tale of lipid medicine; the drug was eventually withdrawn in many countries, while later fibrates are judged on their own trials.
